en: With that [mantra] which has been consecrated seven times with the blazing weapon-mantra, one should mark all the limbs with the letters *a* and *rā*;

having performed *prāṇāyāma* as before, one should release the weapon and meditate upon it as resembling [the deity], remaining there for as long as possible; then, O twice-born, having bathed, one should cross over.
First, one should worship Brāhmī with the two names [namas and abhyām]; thereafter, one should enter into the reality of the Astra-mantra, and indeed into the reality of the other mantras.
Having entered into the midst of the water that bestows a portion of light, [one should hold it] in the left hand.
Having set aside three portions of pure clay— the southern portion with the [mantras] beginning with Śiva,

the eastern portion with the previous mantra, and the northern portion with the *svalaga* [mantra]— and having expelled the obstacles situated in the waters in the various directions by casting the portion of clay over which the mantra has been recited, [one should act] with that which has been consecrated by the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having consecrated the water in the bathing vessels as the sacred *śivatīrtha*, and having touched all parts of the body starting from the head with a portion [of the water], one should bathe while remaining silent and recollecting Śiva; thereafter,
having gone to a clean place, one should rub [the body] with *āmalaka* and so forth using the palm of the left hand.
Having taken water and consecrated it with the root mantra, one should visualize the Moon and Sun, as well as Śakti and Śiva,
in the left and right hands respectively; then, reciting the root mantra and forming the *kumbha-mudrā*,
one should sprinkle [the disciple] while wearing two clean garments and uttering the *praṇava* over water free from bubbles.
Having sipped water three times with the *brāhma* (or *prājāpatya*) *tīrtha* at the base of the thumb using the foam of the water,
one should wipe the lips twice with the base of the thumb;
then, having touched the openings of the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears with the ring finger and the thumb, [one should touch] the right and left [nostrils].

Having sequentially touched the two shoulders and the navel and head with the *darbha* purifiers held in his hands, he should perform worship while seated on a seat (*satvī*). There, having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, he should practice *prāṇāyāma* together with the recitation of the mantra;
then, having placed water for the feet (*pādya*) in his left hand, he should set it down.

Having consecrated [the water] with the six-limbed mantra using the right hand, and having sprinkled oneself with the *kumbha-mudrā* while reciting the root mantra, one should again take water in the left hand and,
with drops of water from that hand, sprinkle each of the [centers] beginning with the heart on the head while reciting the respective mantras.

Having performed the cleansing with the *saṃyojana* [mantra], one should take the remaining water with the right hand, place it at the tip of the ring finger during inhalation, and [visualize] the black form of sin being released. "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya"—
[by this] all conceptual constructions regarding pleasure and pain cease from that very moment.

We shall now proclaim the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), as well as the *kṣā-vidhi* for the Guru, the *pavitrārohaṇa*, and the ritual for that which is devoid of transformation (*vivarta-śūnya*), whose form is pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra-mūrti*).
This very manual for the recollection of daily and other rites has been composed for those men who desire to cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of the boat of [divine] forms.
Now, regarding the procedure for the daily rites: having risen in the morning and performed the necessary duties, one should [cleanse] the Linga with earth during the first watch.
Having washed the left hand, one should wash the anus three times; having washed both [hands] seven times to remove the scent and residue, and having established the state of purity for the gods,
one should wash the feet and hands once with clay, and then [cleanse] with wood.
Having performed the cleansing of the teeth with a twig twelve finger-breadths long and having the girth of the little finger,
one should bathe; having bathed in a river, a confluence, or another such place, and having attended to the necessary bodily functions.
Moving about,
having washed [the hands] while reciting the *śiva-mantra*, one purifies the pure area of ground with the *astra-mantra*; indeed,
having dug [there], one should collect earth with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and [purify it] with the *astra-mantra*.
One should worship there. First, having consecrated the southern [side] with the Astra-mantra, the northern [side] with the Brahma-mantras,
and the center with the Śiva-mantra, and having recited the Astra-mantra over it, one should cast [the water] into the middle of the water with the Vaśa-mudrā while facing the southeast.
Having dried up the water by means of the *dhāraṇā* and having refilled it with nectar (*amṛta*) through another *dhāraṇā*,

one should then conceive of this as the sacred bathing place of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*), using a portion of earth consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra, [extending] from the letter *a* to the letter *ha*.

Having touched all the limbs with a portion consecrated by the *brahmajapta* mantra, and having washed both hands and feet with water mixed with nectar, one should bathe in the middle of the *śivatīrtha*. Then, again,
with the *havanyupacāra* and with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances, [one worships] Śiva with the *brahmāṅga-astra*.

Having performed an ablution upon one's own head with the Śivagāyatrīs accompanied by an ocean of fruits, and having withdrawn the mantras of the true Pāśupata through the grace of the short [vowels], and having drawn them in and placed them within one's own heart via the path of the central channel (*pra-vannāḍī*), one should proceed with the sacrifice.
Even at home, one should prepare a *śivatīrtha* in eight or nine [handfuls] of earth and bathe in that same manner;
or else, having dug up earth eight finger-breadths deep and stirred it... [the rest of the sentence is illegible].

Having spread *darbha* grass facing south, with water mixed with sesame seeds, [he says]: "Oṃ, I offer [this] to Soma, who honors the ancestors, to Yama, to Aṅgiras, to the three Agnis, and to Vyavāhana. Oṃ, I satisfy the hosts of the wives of the ancestors with *svadhā* and obeisance."
Oṃ, I satisfy the hosts of ancestors with *svadhā* and homage. Then, by means of their names and lineages:
Oṃ, I satisfy my own father with *svadhā* and homage; Oṃ, I satisfy my own grandfather with *svadhā* and homage;
Oṃ, I satisfy my own great-grandfather with *svadhā* and homage.
I satiate the mothers with *svadhā*; om, I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā*;
om, I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā*.
Oṃ, I satiate my mother’s great grandfather with *svadhā*. Oṃ, I satiate my mother’s great great-grandfather with *svadhā*.
Oṃ, I satiate my mother’s great great-great-grandfather with *svadhā*.
Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and reverence. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandmothers of my mother with *svadhā* and reverence.
Oṃ, I satiate the great-great-grandmothers of my mother with *svadhā* and reverence.

Thus, the teachers of this tradition do not crush the *pavitraka* [sacred thread]; rather, having discarded it and performed ritual sipping (*ācamana*), they take up another *pavitraka*. Having purified the body with the solar mantra *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ*, and having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, they prepare the vessel of offering (*arghapātra*) and [arrange] the flowers and other items.

Having sprinkled [the area] with red sandalwood and other substances, and having offered *arghya* to the Sun with the root mantra addressed to the Sun, one should worship the Sun. Therein, after the worship of Gaṇapati and the Guru, [one should worship] in the center of the seat with: "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Prabhūta."
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Vimalā; thus in the southeast. Oṃ aṃ, homage to Sārā; thus in the southwest.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Ārādhyā; thus in the northwest.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Paramasukhā—thus in the northeast;
Oṃ aṃ, homage to Padma—thus again in the center;
Oṃ gaṃ, homage to Dīptā—on the eastern petal.
Oṃ rīṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmā in the southeast;
oṃ ruṃ, salutation to Jayā in the south;
oṃ ruṃ, salutation to Bhadrā in the southwest.
Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Vimalā in the east;
oṃ raiṃ, obeisance to Vibhūti in the northwest;
oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to Amoghā in the north.
Oṃ rauṃ, obeisance to Vidyudā; [worship] in the northeast (īśāna).

Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Sarvatomukhī; having worshipped in the pericarp (karṇikā) and displayed the Visphurā mudrā, [one should visualize] a red-colored, circular radiance situated in the center of the universe.

[He should visualize the deity] wearing red garments, seated upon a white lotus, adorned with all ornaments, having one face and two arms, holding a white lotus in his hand, and endowed with all auspicious marks; then,
having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* by means of the expulsion of the earth through the *dvāli* [breath-control] accompanied by tears, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having offered flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other such auspicious items mixed together to Śiva-Sūrya with the mantra "Oṃ Hau Śivasūryāya," one should perform recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity using this very [mantra]. In this manner, one should worship at dawn, at midday, and at evening.
There, at midday, having brought [the deities] from the eastern direction as before, one should satisfy them with mantras and so forth.
There, having performed the *uttarāsaṅga*, one should [offer] the mantras beginning with the *mūlamantra* using the fingertips;
the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and others with the *hṛdaya-mantra* ending in *svāhā*;
Sarasvatī with "Oṃ vāgvādini svāhā"; Indrāṇī with "Oṃ indrāṇyai namaḥ"; and Āgneyī with "Oṃ āgneyyai..."

Homage! Oṃ, homage to Yāmyā. Oṃ, homage to Nairṛtyā. Oṃ, homage to Vāruṇī. Oṃ, homage to Vāyavyā. Oṃ, homage to Saumyā. Oṃ, homage to Aiśānī. Oṃ, homage to Anantā. Oṃ, homage to Nākapaṣṭhā. Thus [are] the directions. Oṃ, to Indra.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ, homage to Yama. Oṃ, homage to [***].
Oṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ, homage to Soma. Oṃ, homage to Brahmā.
Oṃ, homage to Ananta. Thus [ends] the day.
(***********) (? With the joints: Oṃ, I satiate Atri; obeisance! Oṃ, I satiate Viśvāmitra; obeisance! Oṃ, I satiate Pulaha; obeisance! Oṃ, I satiate Kratu;
obeisance! (? I satiate Vasiṣṭha; obeisance! Oṃ, I satiate Marīci; obeisance! Oṃ...
"O Pracetas, I satiate you; salutation!"—thus for the sages (*ṛṣis*). *Oṃ*, I satiate Sanaka; salutation. *Oṃ*, I satiate Sanandana;
salutation. *Oṃ*, I satiate Sanātana; salutation. *Oṃ*, I satiate Sanatkumāra;
salutation. *Oṃ*, I satiate Ṛtu; salutation. Thus.
To humans: Oṃ, salutation to Śiva; Oṃ, salutation to Rudra; Oṃ, salutation to Umāpati;
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā; Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu; Oṃ, salutation to Agni; Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu; Oṃ, salutation to Dharma; Oṃ, salutation to Sūrya; Oṃ, salutation to Candramas.
Thus ends the Siddhāntas.

Oṃ, homage to Āditya. Oṃ, homage to Soma. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāra. Oṃ, homage to Budha. Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati. Oṃ, homage to Cakra. Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. Oṃ, homage to Rāhu. Oṃ, homage to Ketu. Thus [are the offerings] to the planets. Oṃ.

*Vaṣaṭ* to all beings; *namaḥ*. (**********? (!!! Having grasped [the hands] with the two *vaguṇṭhana* [mudrās], one should perform the making of the *śiva*-hand. Therein, beginning from the two big toes, having meditated upon the *suśira* within oneself, [one meditates] upon the *suśira* of the [hand]. (**********)

Having visualized a blazing *hūṃ* syllable in the center of the hollow space (*suśira*), one should restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and fix the mind upon that *hūṃ*. At the end of the exhalation (*recaka*), by means of that very [breath], having turned back toward the Brahma-moon in the middle of the heart-lotus stalk... [the syllable] is established.

Having enveloped the consciousness with the *pūraka* [breath-retention], having placed the *jīva* consisting of the peaceful seed-syllable and the *hūṃkāra* encapsulated within the heart upon the head, and having contemplated the person who is the form of the *jīva*— the solitary *hūṃkāra* bearing the subtle *bindu* at the end of the crest-lock (*śikhā*)— as the supreme reality.
Having performed *kumbhaka*, one should cause the breath to move upward; by means of a single strike, O Śivā, one should unite it with Śiva.

Through the process of *ījavṛtti*, having dissolved [the breath] into Śiva, one should lead it back in reverse order through its respective causes up to the *bindu*. Having led it to the state of non-abiding, one should purify it. Then...

One should purify the elements (*bhūta*) beginning with earth, which are supported by one another and presided over by Īśāna and the other [deities], such as blue and the rest. Therein, the earthly mandala is square, yellow, solid,
marked with a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and consists of the form of the *nivṛtti* kalā, generated from the seed-syllable of earth, *hlāṃ*, starting from the feet.
Having thoroughly contemplated this and purified the form of the wind through various protections,
one should visualize the water-maṇḍala as a half-moon— liquid, gentle, very white, marked with a lotus,
arising from the seed-syllable *hūṃ* in the form of the established *kalā*, and supported by the four fires.
Having purified it as before, the triangular Āgneya-maṇḍala, marked with svastikas and reddish in color, is the form of the Vidyā-kalā by means of the fire-seed syllable *hrūṃ*.
Through three blows, the water-element and the evil should be purified as before. [The Vāyavya...]

The mandala is circular, marked with six dots; having purified it as the element earth—its form being that of the *kalā* of pacification (*śānti*)—by means of the seed-syllables of fire and wind, and by means of the two *udghātas*, one purifies it as before.
Then, by means of the syllable *hūṃ* together with the *ḍha*-sound, it takes the form of space, which is the form of that which transcends pacification (*śāntyatīta*).

Having purified it once as before, one should then cause everything to swell with nectar using the root mantra of the Amṛtavarṣiṇīs. Thus, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), having offered a seat in the heart,
and having projected the pervasive power (*vyāpinī-śakti*) all around, [one should project] the form of the twice-born from the *dvādaśānta*.

Having brought the self, which consists of Śiva, into the pericarp by means of inhalation (pūraka), and having established it there in the form of light and bathed it with nectar, one should perform the purification of the hands. There, having thoroughly cleansed the palms and backs of the hands with sandalwood paste and water, one should rub them together with each other using the *vyasta* (crossed) gesture.

Having honored with a handful of final flowers: *uṃ haṃ khaṃ khasolkāya hrāṃ hrāṃ saḥ*. Having invoked with the invocation-mudrā saying "Salutation to Sūrya," having established and fixed [the deity], one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) and, having restrained [the senses] by means of the placement, [offer] the water for honor (*argha*).
Having offered water for the feet and water for rinsing the mouth with the *khaśolka* vessel, one should worship the void together with its limbs using the root mantra together with its limbs,
using perfumes, flowers, and so forth; then, having displayed the lotus mudrā and the image mudrā, [one worships] the southeast.
*Uṃ Aṃ*, salutation to the heart;

in the northeast (*aiśānī*), *Uṃ Arkādya*, svāhā to the head; in the southwest (*nairṛtī*), *Uṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svar Jvālinī*, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); in the northwest (*vāyavī*), *Uṃ Hūṃ*, hūṃ to the armor (*kavaca*).

Oṃ bhāṃ, vaṣaṭ to the eye, in the center. Having worshipped the limbs with "uṃ raḥ, phaṭ to the weapon" in the four directions starting from the east at the corners, one should perform the *dhenu-mudrā* for the heart and other limbs, the *go-mudrā* for the eye, and the *vṛṣa-mudrā* for the weapon. Then, displaying the *trāsanī-mudrā*, [one recites] "bha pra daśī oṃ saṃ; obeisance to Soma."

At the tip of the eastern petal: *oṃ vuṃ vudhāya namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ vṛṃ vṛhaspataye namaḥ*. In the west: *oṃ bhāṃ bhārgavāya namaḥ*. In the north: *oṃ aṃ aṅgārāya namaḥ*. In the southeast: *oṃ śaṃ śanaiścarāya namaḥ*. In the southwest: *oṃ*...
"Rāṃ, obeisance to Rāhu in the northwest; Oṃ Kaṃ, obeisance to Ketu in the northeast.

Having thus worshipped the planets, having gratified them with the *namaḥsthāra* mudrā, and having offered perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth with the *khaṣolka* mantra, [one should display] the *padma* mudrā and the *vimba* mudrā.

Having displayed [the mudrā], uttered "forgive me," and withdrawn the collection of mantras with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should unite the barley grains situated in the heart with the twelve-syllable [mantra] for the Sun.
Having thus performed the dismissal according to this procedure, one should place the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering) and the water from the *argha* vessel in the northeast.
Salutation to the fierce radiance. [Thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship of the Sun. || 0 ||
Then, having sipped water (ācamana) and performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite, holding the general arghya vessel prepared for the purpose,

he should sprinkle with the Astra-mantra at the door, and at the top of the doorpost, [worship] Gaṇapati and Sarasvatī by their own names, as well as Svarga and the rivers Nandā and Aṅgā, and Mahākāla and Yamunā, along with himself.

Having worshipped [the deities] on the right and left with their respective names preceded by the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should cast a flower inside the sacrificial hall using the application of the flaming *nārāca* weapon to expel obstacles; then,
placing the heel there and leaning slightly against the northern branch.
Without touching the threshold with his right foot,

having entered inside, he should scatter flowers for the purpose of warding off obstacles; then, having offered a flower at the Brahma-sthāna with "oṃ vāstoṣpataye brahmaṇe namaḥ," he should [offer] at the seat with "oṃ anantāsanāya namaḥ."
As stated in the *Śāstra*: "Oṃ pracodayāt... [restored] ...nivṛttiṃ on the western face.
Thus, these are the four *kalās* of Tatpuruṣa. "Oṃ aghorebhyo namaḥ" [restored] ...mohāṃ.

To the neck: *Oṃ ghora namaḥ*—to Hunger (*kṣayā*) on the right shoulder. *Oṃ ghorataraśca namaḥ*—to Thirst (*niṣṭhā*) on the left shoulder. *Oṃ sarvataḥsarva namaḥ*—with the pervasive mantra [to] the [senses] (*bhā*). *Oṃ bhūtebhyo namaḥ*—to Death (*mṛtyu*) in the belly. *Oṃ namaste rudra namaḥ*—to Hunger (*kṣudhā*).

On the back: *Oṃ rūpābhyo namaḥ*. On the chest of Tṛṣā: the eight *kalās* of Aghora. On the anus: *Oṃ vāmāya namaḥ*. On the thighs: *Oṃ jyeṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. On the right thigh: *Oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*. On the [left] thigh: *Oṃ kālāya namaḥ*.

On the left upper arm: *oṃ kalāyai namaḥ*. On the right knee: *oṃ vikaraṇyai namaḥ*. On the left knee: *oṃ balavikaraṇyai namaḥ*. On the right buttock: *oṃ balāyai namaḥ*. On the [left] buttock: *oṃ pramathanīyai namaḥ*. [And] on the [left] hip: *oṃ vṛddhyai namaḥ*.

On the left buttock: *Oṃ sarvabhṛta samanāya namaḥ*; thus, Bhrāmaṇī on the waist. *Oṃ mana namaḥ*; thus, Trimohanī on the right side. *Oṃ unmanāya namaḥ*; thus, Jvarā on the left side. These are the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva.
"Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation"—with this, [one attains] *siddhi* on the right foot.
"Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta"—with this, [one attains] *dadvi* on the left foot. "Oṃ, salutation to Bhava"—with this, [one attains] *dyuti* on the right hand.
Oṃ abhava namaḥ—thus [he places] Lakṣmī on the left hand;
Oṃ anādibhave namaḥ—thus Medhā on the nose;
Oṃ bhajasvamā namaḥ—thus Kārti on the head.
"Oṃ bhava namaḥ"—with this, [he places] Svadhā on the right arm;
"Oṃ udbhava namaḥ"—with this, Nidhṛti on the left arm.
Thus, according to the Sadyojāta ritual, [these are placed] upon the arms with their respective mudrās, starting from Īśāna.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*), having brought about the body of consciousness (*vidyādeha*), and having invoked the root mantra, one should place the heart-mantra on the heart, the head-mantra on the head, the crest-mantra on the crest, the armor-mantra on all limbs, and the weapon-mantra on the hand.

Having performed the act of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), one should perform the three claps of the hand with the *mahāmudrā*, the snapping of fingers, the gazing, and the threatening gesture; then, having purified the site with the *astra-mantra* against obstacles residing in that place, the clearing of the directions, and the *avaguṇṭhana* [covering], one should effect the purification of the location (*sthāna-śuddhi*).

Having performed the heart-worship as in the external sacrifice, and having completed the internal sacrifice ending with meditation at the center of the brows through the fire-oblation at the navel, one should burn the vessel for the special *argha* offering with the *astra-mantra*, purify it by washing, and then project the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*)— which has the luster of my own [the teacher's] body and terminates in Śakti— into that vessel; then, one should worship Śiva with the root-mantra (*mūla*).
With the outer thumbs [one worships] Īśāna; with the index fingers, Tatpuruṣa; with the middle fingers, Aghora; with the ring fingers, Vāmadeva; with the little fingers, Sadyojāta.
Then, with the little fingers [one worships] the Heart; with the ring fingers, the Head; and with the middle fingers, the Topknot (Śikhā).

Having placed the armor upon the index finger and the entrails between the two thumbs, one should join them with the subsequent *rajas*, envelop them in armor, and employ them in all rites. In every case, having performed purification of the hands by this method from the sipping of water onwards, [one should perform] the *kṣarakandhapikā*.

Having bound the *liṅgamudrā* on oneself, one should say: "May Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Brahman, the Auspicious One, Sadāśiva, be [present] forever.
Then, having formed the fist of Īśāna with the tip of the thumb in the *bhadramudrā*, one should place it upon the head.
"Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra impel us.
In the same manner, by joining the middle finger with the thumb, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the mouth.
"Oṃ, from the non-terrible ones, from the terrible ones, from those more terrible than the terrible, [protect] us, O Śarva, from all sides."
With the mantra "śarva-sarvebhyo namas-te rudra-rūpebhyaḥ," he should place the Aghora-mantra at the heart using the union of the middle finger and the thumb;
[and] with "oṃ vāmadevāya namo jyeṣṭhāya namo rudrāya namaḥ kālāya namaḥ."
“Homage to the one who effects transformation; homage to the subduer of strength; homage to the tamer of all beings;
homage to the one who transcends the mind. With this, by joining the thumb and ring finger, one should worship the deity of the name at the secret place.
“Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; homage indeed to Sadyojāta.”
With the mantra "bhave bhave nātibhave bhajasva māṃ bhavodbhavāya," one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) by joining the little finger and the thumb,
starting from the feet and extending up to the head; thus, having placed Sadyojāta as the pervasive embodiment throughout the entire body according to the Brahmā-arrangement, [one proceeds] upward.
Then, by means of facial expressions on the faces facing the northeast, south, west, and [the others],
and by means of the ritual sequence, [he places] "Oṃ Īśāna, obeisance to all vidyās" as Śaśinī on the crown; and "Oṃ Īśvara, obeisance to all beings" as Aṅgadā on the eastern crown.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of Brahman"—with this, [one should place] the desired Śivā on the eastern head; "obeisance to Marīci"—on the northern head;
"Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva"—Jvālinī on the western head.

Thus, the five kalās of Īśāna are [as follows]: the unmanifest (avyakta) kalā is "Oṃ, we know Tatpuruṣa; obeisance"—this is the Peace (śānti), at the eastern face as before. "Oṃ, we meditate on the seven gods; obeisance"—this is Knowledge (vidyā), at the southern face.
Having worshipped [the deities] among the humans in the petals of the directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast, one should worship in the pericarp:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Manātmananī" and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala)."
Oṃ hāṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya [namaḥ]—thus at the tips of the petals.
Oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ.
Oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ—thus at the tips of the filaments.

"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala," and "obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala"— thus [one offers salutation] in the pericarp. Having meditated upon the seat pervaded by the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Śuddhavidyā.
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one whose self is Śiva"— thus worship Śiva. Then,
having formed a handful of flowers, "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva"— thus,
having projected the form (*mūrti*), perform there the ritual projection (*nyāsa*) of the Brahma-face according to the prescribed method.
Again, with hands joined in *añjali* with flowers, [he visualizes] Padmāsana,
sixteen years of age, five-faced, with his right hands displaying the *prasāda*, the *śakti*, the trident, and the *khaṭvāṅga*.
With his ten left hands holding a serpent, a rosary, a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a lotus, a blue water-lily (*utpala*), and a citron (*bījapūra*), he is exceedingly gracious with a smiling face;
his matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) are adorned with three eyes representing the triad of the powers of knowledge and action.

Having meditated upon [the deity] adorned with the crescent moon of knowledge, one should perform the placement of the *vidyādeha* (knowledge-body) with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*.
Again, having filled the heart-mantra with flowers until it is full, one should first [worship] Sadyojāta.

Having recited the root mantra, one should lead the mass of radiating rays to the *dvādaśānta* and become absorbed in that essence. Having meditated on the arising of the *bindu* in its place, and having taken [the deity] from there with a steady mind, one should invoke [the deity] into the image by means of the *āvāhana-mudrā*. Then, through the path of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [one should unite it] with the *liṅga*.
Having established [the deity] through *sthāpanī*, having brought it close through *saṃnidhānī* with its manifold form,
and having caused it to abide through *saṃnirodhanī* with the *aniṣṭharā* [mudrā], one should cover [it] with the Heart-mantra or the Armor-mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*,
and offer the *argha* at the feet while facing the deity.

Having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *mukha* mantra, and water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*) with the *hṛdaya* or the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, having given these to Śiva and performed a welcome, one should provide the meatless unguents and baths; then, for the purpose of the ritual bathing, having taken the jars, having sprinkled them with water, struck them, and consecrated them with the *astra* mantra.
Having consecrated the bathing water in the vessels as the *śivatīrtha* with the *mantrasaṃhitā* or with purifying [mantras],

and having agitated the water with the *astra-mantra*, one should wash the cloth up to the end of the water-pot (*gaḍuka*). Then, with the filtered water and either the *gāyatrī* or the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer drops [of water] together with the *vardhanī* vessel for the *astra*.

Having filled [the vessel] with water from the meditation on the form of the nectar of immortality, along with flowers, *dūrvā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), accompanied by the mantra; having worshipped it and performed the *dhenumudrā*, having veiled it with the ritual action of the *avaguṇṭhana*, and having consecrated the supreme self upon the head with the *tantra*... he [should do so].
Having sprinkled items such as flowers and the like with water from the *kukuśa* vessel for the sake of purification using the *astra-mantra*,

having sprinkled them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having consecrated them with the *hṛdaya-mantra* or the *piṇḍa-mantras*; or else, one should consecrate the ointment with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the garment with the *śiras-mantra*, and the collection of ornaments with the *śikhā-mantra*.
The food offering (naivedya) with the Kavaca mantra; flowers with the Mūla mantra; milk, curd, and so forth with the Kavaca mantra;
clarified butter (ghṛta) with the Śikhā mantra; honey (kṣaudra) with the Śiras mantra; and sugar-candy (khaṇḍa) with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having consecrated the scented water and applied a tilaka mark on one's own head with sandalwood paste, [one should offer it].
One should offer a flower with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having observed the appropriate silence as desired,

and having performed the purification of the mantra through the utterance of the mantras accompanied by the *pluta* (protracted) vowels, one should worship the previously arranged offering (*pūjā*) with the *gāyatrī*, and present the general offering of water (*argha*) for self-surrender.

Having repeated the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta, one should remove the worship from the liṅga and, using the *hṛdayamantra*, cast it onto Caṇḍeśa who resides on the pedestal in the northeast. Then, having washed the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra* and having washed the liṅga, this constitutes the purification of the liṅga.

One should perform [the rite]. Everywhere, one should worship Śiva, whose limbs consist of the fivefold indicators of the mantra, with the self as the support. There, on the pedestal in the southeast, [one says]: *Oṃ gauṃ gaṇādhipataye namaḥ*.
In the northeast, [one says]: *Oṃ hāṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*. This is the general *arghya* offering.

Having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes, [one should say]: "Obeisance to the power that is the source of the body. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta; in the center. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma; in the southeast (āgneyī). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jvālā; in the southwest (nairṛtī). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya; in the northwest (vāyavyā).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sovereignty (aiśvarya) in the northeast. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Unrighteousness (adharma) in the east. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ignorance (ajñāna) in the south. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Non-detachment (avairāgya) in the west. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to True Sovereignty (saiśvarya).
Having worshipped in the north in the presence of Jñāna: *oṃ hāṃ adhaśchadanāya namaḥ*. In the presence of Aiśvarya: *oṃ hāṃ ūrddhvandhadanāya namaḥ*. In the center, however:
*oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. [To] Valavikaraṇī: *namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ bala*...
Salutation to Pramathanī. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī.
These are the eight Śaktis. [End of section]. Then, near the Kuśa grass, [the ritual] is performed with the Śiva-mantra as prescribed; there is sprinkling with the Astra-mantra.
Striking with the *kavaca* [armor-mantra], scraping with the *astra* [weapon-mantra], scattering, filling, leveling, and likewise smoothing;
then, having prepared the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by sprinkling and cleansing it, one should expand it.
With three lines oriented north-south and four lines together with a transverse line, [the diagram is formed].

Having offered each of the four *jīkaraṇa* substances, one should worship the omnipresent Lord with *arghya* using the two-fold [mantras]. Then, one should bathe Him with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth. Having rinsed Him and wiped Him dry, one should again bathe Him with pure water according to one's capacity, using pure water alone.

Having bathed [the deity] with scented water and the root-mantra, and having wiped it dry with a clean cloth, one should first offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and then offer water for the head (*śirovāri*). Thereafter, one should again provide a seat, garments, ointments, ornaments such as jewelry, and various pure, fragrant flowers. Oṃ.

Having worshipped the deity with "Hlauṃ? Śivāya namaḥ" and having fully honored the Brahmamantras according to the prescribed placement (nyāsa): Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the head. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor (kavaca). Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes. Oṃ...
Having worshipped [the limbs] with "Haḥ astrāya phaṭ" on the [respective] parts of the body; having worshipped Īśāna in the center, and Tatpuruṣa and the others in the east, south, north, and west;
and having worshipped the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest; [then] in the east and south...
Having worshipped the one situated in the northwest and offered perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should sprinkle the incense vessel with the *astra-mantra*, worship it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, consecrate it with the *dhenumudrā*, and then,
having worshipped it with the *astra-mantra*, one should offer it while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, radiant lights, and so forth, and having placed *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and the sacred thread upon the head of the deity, one should remove the *rātrika* covering and perform the *pañcāṅga* [prostration] according to one's ability.
Furthermore, having obtained the auspicious threefold path from the Lord of Beings (*Bhavat*), therein—

The *mānasa* (mental) [japa] is that which is accomplished through the activity of the mind alone; it is self-perceived and whispered (*upāṃśu*), yet not heard by others, being internal in the form of mental discourse. That which is heard by others is the *sabhāṣya* (articulated). Furthermore, these correspond respectively to the superior, middling, and inferior levels of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
For one whose mind is not properly disciplined through rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and prosperity (*puṣṭi*), [the practice] is not accomplished because it is difficult to achieve;

since it has the attainment of the lower [levels] as its fruit, it is whispered (*upāṃśu*). It is common to all fruits and should be employed in three ways: neither too fast, nor too slow, neither lacking eight syllables, nor otherwise.

In the case of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the reciters should perform the mental recitation (*manasajapa*) facing either east or north. In rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), it should be performed according to the particular wish; in rites such as malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*), it may even be performed facing another direction. In that regard, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) by whichever means possible. Then, one should fully worship the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).

Having worshipped that [deity]— who is enveloped in armor and protected within— with scented water mixed with *kuśa* grass, flowers, sandalwood, and *akṣata* (unbroken rice), in a vessel upon a lotus whose petals and filaments extend from the east to the northeast, one should recite: *oṃ hāṃ manotmananyai*.

Homage in the pericarp: *oṃ hāṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* (homage to the solar disc). *oṃ hāṃ sūryamaṇḍalādhipataye bahurūpāya namaḥ* (homage to Bahurūpa, the lord of the solar disc)—thus at the tips of the petals. *oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* (homage to the lunar disc). *oṃ hāṃ somamaṇḍalādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ* (homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc).

Thus, on the tips of the filaments: *oṃ hāṃ agnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. On the pericarp: *oṃ hāṃ agnimaṇḍalādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ*. Having meditated upon the seat pervaded by the principles from Earth up to Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*), [one offers] *oṃ hāṃ śivāsanāya*.

One should worship the Śivāsana with the mantra "Namaḥ. Then, filling the joined palms (añjali) with flowers, one should install the form (mūrti) with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva. Having thus performed the installation of the form, one should duly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Brahmā-face therein. Again, [filling] the joined palms with flowers... [Brahma].

Seated in the lotus posture, casting a limited shadow, appearing about sixteen years of age, with five faces, and possessing ten arms— his right hands holding the *abhaya* gesture, a trident, and a *khaṭvāṅga*; his left hands likewise holding a snake, an eye, a rosary, a *ḍamaru* drum, a *nīla* flower, and a *bījapura* fruit.
Having made the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) very serene with a smiling face by means of the *astramantra*, one should spread darbha grass around it, with their tips pointing east and north,
having a circumference of eight finger-breadths.

Having placed thirty enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *darbha* grass, each one cubit in length, or having wound them around, and having arranged the ritual seats (*viṣṭara*) in the four directions starting from the one to be worshipped, proceeding clockwise while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should worship the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the mantra:
"Oṃ, salutation to Kalākuṇḍa. Then, one should worship Vāgīśvarī, who is intent on [the sacrifice].

Having meditated upon Gīśvara as possessing desire, having invoked him and worshipped him with the *dhruva* mantra, and having secured the axle-socket with the *astra* mantra, one should bring fire from a forest, from a solar stone (*sūryakānta*), from the house of a twice-born (*dvija*), from the house of a Vaiśya, or from a well-built house, [excluding] that which consumes raw flesh.

Having set aside the arghya-vessel from his hand, having sprinkled [the area] and veiled it with the *kavaca* mantra, and having placed the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*) while reciting "Oṃ rauṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire" (*agnicaitanya*),
one should consecrate the fire with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* and having worshipped it, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times; then, kneeling upon the ground and facing oneself,
one should cast a drop of water into the channel (*nāḍī*) of the Goddess of Speech (*Vāgīśvarī*) while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having recited the *Savitri* mantra over a bracelet for the protection of the fetus,

and having taken it from the hand of the Goddess with the *astra-mantra*, [he should wear it] for the sake of conception; then, for the sake of the *puṃsavana* rite, he should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having worshipped with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should offer three oblations; having worshipped with the Śrī [mantra] for the sake of the sign, one should worship with the Dhāraṇā [mantra] and offer three oblations with the Śikhā [mantra];
having worshipped with the Tatpuruṣa mantra for the purpose of birth, one should offer three oblations with the Kavaca [mantra] for the purpose of the naming ceremony.

Having worshipped with the Īśāna mantra and offered three oblations with the Astra mantra, one should give the fire the name "Śivāgni" (the Fire of Śiva) using the root mantra, saying "O Hutāśana," and then perform the dismissal of the Father. Once this is done, for the cessation of the impurity of death, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water from the *argha* vessel for the protection of the fire.

Having strewn *darbha* grass with its tips pointing east and north while reciting the *astreṇa* mantra, and having opened the mouths [of the fire] with three oblations, one should take up the *lālāpa* for the sake of nourishment; and for the sake of growth,
[one should offer] sixteen-fold portions smeared with ghee, measuring the length of the arms, from the root to the tip.
Having performed the oblation with five or twenty-four [verses],
and having worshipped the guardians of the world (lokapālas) upon the girdle, the sacrificial grass, and the enclosing sticks— Brahmā in the east, Rudra in the south, and [Viṣṇu] in the west—
Having praised Viṣṇu, one should worship Īśvara. Then,
with wood such as *śrīparṇī*, one should fashion a staff (*daṇḍa*) thirty-six finger-breadths in length,
with a circumference of six finger-breadths at its base, and four finger-breadths at the tip.

One should offer [the recitation] with three verses, saying: "May this be the means for the attainment of my fruit for the sake of Śiva. "O You, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by me. May it lead to my success through Your grace; I abide in You."
O God, whatever we do, whether good or evil deeds,
destroy that for me while I abide in the state of Śiva— HŪṂ KṢAḤ, O Śaṅkara!
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva performs the sacrifice everywhere, and I myself am indeed Śiva.

Having thus offered the recitation (*japa*), the worship (*pūjā*), and oneself as an oblation to the God Śiva, and having meditated upon and praised Him as previously described, one should perform a prostration with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-namaskṛti*) using the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra-mudrā*). Then, for the sake of the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one should prepare] a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) possessing the characteristics as stated.

One should go near that place and construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)—either square or circular for all purposes, or according to specific desires—as a triangle, a semi-circle, a hexagon, an octagon, a sixteen-sided figure, or a *śivā* [shape]. For a homa of fifty [oblations], it should be one *muṇḍa-hasta* in measure; for a homa of one hundred [oblations], it should be one *ratni* in measure.
For a thousand oblations, [the pit] is one cubit; for ten thousand oblations, two cubits; for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits;
for a million oblations, six cubits; and for ten million oblations, eight cubits.
It should be equal in depth, length, and width, and likewise above in the case of the girdles (*mekhalā*).

For the *muṇḍa* hand-measure, the first [line] is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the second is one *aṅgula*, and the third is half an *aṅgula*. For the *ratni* measure, they are three, two, and one *aṅgula* respectively. For the *hasta* measure, they are four, three, and two *aṅgulas*.
For a two-cubit [kuṇḍa], they are six, four, and three finger-breadths; for a four-cubit [kuṇḍa], they are six, four, and [three] finger-breadths;

for a six-cubit [kuṇḍa], they are ten, eight, and six finger-breadths; and for an eight-cubit [kuṇḍa], they are twelve, ten, and eight finger-breadths. In all kuṇḍas, according to this sequence, there are three triangular girdles (mekhalās).

The girdles (mekhalā) should be fashioned in the very shape of the pit; they should be located either to the south or the west (vāruṇī) of the pit, circular in the middle like the pit itself or shaped like an aśvattha leaf,
twelve aṅgulas in length, eight aṅgulas in width, with a lip two aṅgulas high.

For the first *kuṇḍa*, the *yoni* should be fashioned with an increase of two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) for each of the remaining ones. Then, having sat down near the *kuṇḍa*, one should perform the inspection of the *kuṇḍa* with the *Śiva-mantra*,
the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the *astra-mantra*, the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with the *kavaca-mantra*, and the scraping (*ullekhana*) with the *tāta-nama-astra-mantra*.

Filling, leveling, sprinkling, cutting, sweeping, and smearing; the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); three lines extending eastward or northward, joined with a transverse line to form a group of four, the formation of the thunderbolt (vajra), and the laying out of the crossroads.
Having joined [the deity], worshipped him, and veiled him with the *kavaca*, one should offer three oblations for the sake of his presence.

Then, having sprinkled the disciple at the region of the heart, and having entered his heart by way of the *ātman* while uttering the syllable *huṃ* through the application of exhalation (*recaka*) from another [channel] using the flower-weapon (*puṣpāstra*), one should enter.
Having pierced the consciousness of the child— which has the form of a shimmering star— within the heart with the Astra-mantra,

and having visualized it with the Mūla-mantra, one should enclose the heart within the *dvādaśānta* (the twelve-finger space above the head). Then, having gathered it with the *saṃhāramudrā* using the mantra *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*, one should join it to the thread as the pervasive [consciousness].

Having honored [the deity] and veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root-mantra for the purpose of depositing [the deity]. Furthermore, one should perform the striking (*tāḍana*) and other rites upon the thread of the fetters (*pāśa*), not upon the body. Thereafter, [one should consider] the fetters as consisting of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and illusion (*māyā*), and not as the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).

Having observed that the *bhoga-śarīra* (enjoyment-body), the objects, and the progenitor are not bound by the thread, one should unite them with the consciousness residing in the thread within the *śāntyatītā* [kalā] and the others. Having struck the disciple on the head with the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītāyai huṃ phaṭ" and having grasped him with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, [one should recite] "Oṃ hauṃ".

"Salutation to Śāntyatītā"—with these words, one should apply [the mantra] to the thread. Thereafter, with "Oṃ hyaiṃ śāntyai huṃ phaṭ," one should strike the thread at two finger-breadths from the end with the Astra-mantra; then, having gathered it by means of the Saṃhāra-mudrā through the process of inhalation (pūraka), one applies "Oṃ hyaiṃ śāntyai namaḥ" to the thread.

One should join it. Thereafter, having struck the *galakānna* at its end with the Flower-Arrow mantra (*puṣpāstra*), one should collect it with the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāramudrā*) while reciting *oṃ hrūṃ vidyāyai huṃ phaṭ*, and then join the thread while reciting *oṃ hrīṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. Again, [one should strike] from the secret part to the end with the Flower-Arrow mantra.

Having struck it with "Oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttyai huṃ phaṭ," one should collect it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and join it to the thread with "Oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ. Having thus performed the striking, collecting, and joining, one should contemplate the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). That is the reality (*tattva*).

The world-planes (*bhuvana*), words (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and mantras are pervaded by the stainless *māyā-karma*; furthermore, the impurities (*mala*) and so forth are the pervaders, while the levels of reality such as Śānti and Atīta are the pervaded by the *kalās*. Therefore, when these [levels] are grasped, the principles (*tattva*) and the impurities (*mala*) are also thereby grasped.

"Those who have been attended to by those who have been attended to become pure even through the pure. Therefore, he says: "Then, having divided [the area] into four parts and given one part to the two sides, [one should give] half a part..."
Having rotated from the center through the end of the three outer angles, it takes the form of a half-moon and a bow.
Having divided the square into four parts, and having increased one part on each side,

one should decrease one part below the *brahmasthāna*; then, having rotated the increased portion by half a part like a crescent moon, the middle [portion] for the sake of the staff (*daṇḍa*) shall consist of three parts.
Having given half of the staff and honey, the circle [is formed] at the sound "ṭaṃ". || 0 ||

Having divided a square into four parts and given half of the field to each side for the root of the tusk, one should make a curve at the front from the third part; thus the support for the root of the tusk should be fashioned on the elephant tusk.
Having given a third part of the square at the front and having given a sixth part on both sides, one should join two threads at the marks; thus, by means of three equal lines, it becomes a triangle.
In a square, having given six parts on both sides of the Brahma-sūtra, a hexagon is formed by drawing equal lines from the center through the four resulting "fish" (matsya) points using equal cords.
In the four fish-diagrams as well, by means of drawing lines in the sequence of triangles, a hexagon is formed.

Having led the cord measuring half the diagonal outside from the square, one should divide the remainder of the square into three parts; by omitting one part and drawing a circle by rotation from the Brahma-sthāna [the center], [the mandala is formed].
In the mandalas where the lotus-doors have not been specifically designated, there are particular characteristics; the state [of these] at the lotus-doors is like that of the Sarvatobhadra.
Having completed one of these mandalas, beginning with the entry into the mandala,

and having performed the rites up to the seating of the disciples in the southern sector of the mandala, the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and the satiation with mantras (*mantra-tarpaṇa*), and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
The bathing (*snapana*) of the mantras beginning with the root mantra and ending with the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) should be performed with the following:
*oṃ huṃ hlauṃ huṃ phaṭ* | *oṃ huṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ* | *oṃ huṃ hīṃ huṃ*.

*phaṭ* | *oṃ huṃ hluṃ h huṃ phaṭ* | *oṃ huṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ* | *oṃ huṃ haḥ phaṭ*. These are the expressive mantras (*vācakāḥ*), ending in a harsh sound; they are to be applied together with colored powders (*rajas*) as the objects of expression (*vācyāḥ*). With knitted brows and terrifying faces, they are to be employed for binding with nooses and other rites of all mantras.

The illumination (*dīpana*) should be performed with three oblations for each [of the three]. Thereafter, a thread fashioned from a girl’s [hair], tripled and then tripled again [to make nine strands], sprinkled with water, and veiled by the *kavaca* mantra, should be worshipped and placed upon the crown of the disciple’s head, which is half the size [of his body].

Having meditated on the form of the *nāḍī*, one should grasp the *suṣumnā* within the disciple’s body with the mantra “Oṃ, obeisance to Suṣumnā,” according to the *Padagṛhyasūtra*. Whether [the disciple] has attained [realization] a hundred times or not, whether he is desirous of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) or desirous of liberation (*mumukṣu*), it is likewise for him at the eastern head.

Having protected the disciple’s right head with the *astra* mantra and others while reciting the *śuddhahasmāna*, and having placed [the syllables] upon the heart, the middle, and the crest using the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should cover him with a garment over which the *varma-mantra* has been recited and let him sleep.
Outside the bed, one should draw three lines with sesame, mustard seeds, and ashes consecrated with mantras.

Having performed the external ritual (bāhyaliṅga) and offered [the oblation], and having consumed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth together with the initiated ones like a disciple, O King, he should then rise in the morning and, having completed the rules for his daily rites, seek permission from the Lord facing eastward.

Having summoned the disciple who is to be sacrificed, if [the omen] is inauspicious, a pacifying *homa* must be performed for the sake of the creation of the vision; however, if it is auspicious, having performed the rites such as the entry of the disciple as previously described,
he should be brought near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having fastened the *pāśasūtra*, [one should perform] the favoring of the victim (*paśu*).

Having reflected, "I am performing [this]," one should first place the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti) in the form of a blazing flame of fire. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Support-Energy.* Above that is Nivṛtti;
its seed-syllable is *pīḍi*, its vowel is *v* (or *ī*), its consonant is *kṣa*, and its steps are twenty-eight.

There are one hundred and eight *purāṇas*. Having deposited these and contemplated the *nivṛtti-kalā* that pervades them, one should worship them with scents, flowers, and so forth, while reciting: "Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to the *nivṛtti-kalā*," and having grasped [the essence] with this, one should place it within the fire.

Having offered three oblations with "Oṃ hlāṃ, svāhā to the *nivṛtti* level (*kalā*)," one should contemplate the three bonds (*pāśas*)— consisting of impurity (*mala*), action (*karman*), and illusion (*māyā*)— which produce the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and the body of experience (*bhoga-śarīra*). Thereafter, one should conceive of the hundreds of infinite sound-matrices (*dhvani-yoni*) beginning with Rudra and ending with Ananta.

One should invoke and worship the goddess Vāgīśvarī, who pervades that [deity], by means of the heart-mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ vāgīśvarī namaḥ*. Thereafter, having led her in with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and offered three oblations with *oṃ vāgīśvaryai svāhā*, one should pray: "O Blessed One, for the sake of the grace of the bound soul (*paśu*), be present here. Thus.

Having sprinkled the disciple with the disciple-mantra and empowered him, one should strike his heart with *oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, entering his body through one's own exhalation (*recaka*), one should sever the heart with the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
extract [the consciousness] by means of the *vaśamudrā*, and while recollecting the root-mantra, lead it to the *dvādaśānta*.

Having meditated on [the consciousness] in the form of a drop on the tip of a blade of grass, having encapsulated it with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having placed the consciousness of the bound soul (*paśu*) within one's own heart by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*) through the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, reciting "Oṃ Haṃ," and having performed the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), remember the root mantra; by this very means, [it reaches] the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
Having led [them] forth and grasped them with the *bhavamudrā*, by means of the manifold individual forms residing in all wombs (*yoni*),

the grasping of the *kalās* of the vehicles (*viyāna*), as well as the grasping of the impurities (*mala*) such as *ādhāra*, *tattva*, and so forth, is accomplished. Thus, the worship of the nooses (*pāśa*) situated in the *sūtrasthāna* is performed with their own respective mantras.

Having performed [the preliminary rites], the illumination of the ritual procedure (*vidhāyadīpana*) should be performed: Oṃ hūṃ hauḥ śāntyatītāyai hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hyaḥ śāntyai hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hrūṃ vidyāyai hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hvīṃ pratiṣṭhāyai hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hlā nivṛttyai |

*Huṃ huṃ phaṭ!* Having thus performed the kindling with three oblations each, one should effect the binding of the fetters (*pāśas*). Then, having struck the head with the *astra-mantra*, [one recites]: *Oṃ hauṃ hauṃ hauṃ, O Blessed One, Śāntyatīta, [bind] the fetter of impurity and karma.*

One should tie a knot in the thread with the mantra "tatvabhuvanādivyāpakam bandhaya hūṃ phaṭ. Thereafter, having struck the region of the forehead with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should say: "Oṃ hau hyaṃ! O Blessed One, bind the noose of the *śāntikalā*, which consists of impurity (*mala*) and so forth, and pervades the principles (*tattva*) and so forth; hūṃ phaṭ! (2)
One should make a knot in the thread according to the *sūtra*. Then, having struck the thread on the throat with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should make a knot in the thread with the mantra:
*oṃ hauṃ hrūṃ bhagavan vidyāpāśaṃ malādi tattvādi vyāpa bandha huṃ phaṭ*. Then, [one should strike] the thread at the navel with the weapon-mantra.
Having struck it with "Oṃ hauṃ hvīṃ hauṃ bhagavan pratiṣṭhāpāśaṃ malādi tattvādi vyāpakaṃ bandha (2) phaṭ," one should make a knot in the thread.
Thereafter, having struck the thread with the Astra-mantra, [one recites] "Oṃ hauṃ hlāṃ hauṃ."

"O Blessed One, [I offer] the noose of the collection of fetters, which pervades the impurities and the principles (tattvas); [I perform] the binding: *huṃ phaṭ*. Thus one should make a knot in the thread. Then, having placed [the substance] from the noose within a pair of shallow bowls (*sarāva*), one should perform the *saṃpāta* oblations. Then, upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), [one prepares] the maṇḍala.

For the purpose of protecting the offering presented to the *liṅga*, one should present it in the *śivakumbha*. One should perform the illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantras as well as the suspension of the thread (*sūtrāvalambana*). This involves the union with the *suṣumnā* channel and the joining of the disciple’s consciousness (*caitanya*). Then, the intention regarding impurities (*mala*), karma, and so forth, proceeds sequentially from the *śāntyatīta* kalā downwards.

Striking, seizing, union, worship, satiation, and illumination; binding, the transcendence of peace (śāntyatītā), and the offering of the Śiva-vessel—this is the sequence of ritual action for the binding of the fetters (pāśabandha) taught by Śiva. Then, [the teacher should perform] the disciple’s [union] with Śiva, Śambhu, the vessel, and the fire...

Having caused [the disciples] to perform prostrations and having seated them in three mandala-circles outside the pavilion, one should sequentially give them the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-stick (dantadhāvana). Regarding the dropping of the tooth-stick, it occurs in the east, north, northeast, and west; elsewhere, it is not so.

For the sake of pacifying a fall, one hundred and eight oblations are offered. Then, for the purification of transgressions (*prāyaścitta*), one hundred and eight oblations are offered with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Upon pure ground, [the ritual proceeds] with *darbha* grass and the *śānti* [mantra], accompanied by the *astra* [mantra].

Having prepared the middle and victorious [oblations], and having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of completing the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), [one should proceed] for the sake of the sacrificial pap (*caru*).

Having drawn out fire for the purpose of incense and lamps from within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having brought it back after the consecration of the pit, one should worship it every day. Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations in that very pit, one should daily obstruct the harsh womb or generate [the fire] there.

Immediately thereafter, having invoked the Blessed One seated upon the heart-lotus of the fire and having worshipped him together with his limbs, one should effect the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) between Śiva residing in the fire and Śiva present at the sacrifice; then,

according to one's inclination, [one should perform] the limb-worship (*aṅga*) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) ten times the required portion (*daśāṃśa*) through whichever face [of the deity] is desired.

One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). The materials for that oblation are: sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), milk, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey, curd, sesame seeds, barley, rice, various kinds of food, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), side-dishes (*vyañjana*), boiled vegetables, roasted vegetables, tubers, roots, fruits, and so forth. Regarding the measure of the oblations therein:

Substances such as honey, milk, and ghee are measured with a *śruva* ladle. For curd and milk, the measure is one *prasṛti*. For root-born substances, it is divided into three parts. For solid food, it is according to what is produced;
for *harītakī* and similar items, it is equal to a *dyā* [or *yava*]; for liquids, it is the size of a joint; and for ascetics (*varṇin*), it is two finger-breadths.

The fruits, flowers, and leaves should be unbroken; they should be possessed of vitality and free from defects such as wounds. The fuel-sticks should be neither too small nor too large, measuring a span (prādeśa) in length, and mixed with condiments, forest products, and oil-cakes.

A quantity of cow dung the size of a village, or rice with its crest intact; subsequently, a collection of rice, barley, and so forth, equal to the hollow of a palm; a handful of sesame, parched grain flour, and the like, the size of a doe;
and a paste of guggulu the size of a jujube stone, along with saffron, sandalwood, and *hastarikā*.

The portion of camphor and other such substances is the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*). For the eight-limbed bulbous roots (*kanda*) of jasmine (*jātī*), it is the measure of a well-extended palm. For leafy vegetables (*śāka*), it is the same as the palm. For parched grain (*lāja*), it is a mere handful, measured by extending the index and little fingers and joining the tips of the middle, ring, and thumb fingers.
The *sūkarī* [mudrā] consists of the tips of the five fingers joined together in the shape of a bud.

In this manner, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the seed-syllables (*bīja*), words (*pada*), and mantras (*brahman*). Then, having filled the *śruk* ladle with clarified butter (*ājya*), placing the *śruva* ladle over it with its opening facing downward, and having placed a flower at its tip—
Holding both [the tips] together like a conch shell with the left and right hands,
standing with feet even and raising them equally,
having placed them crosswise upon the navel while reciting the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, with the gaze fixed on the tips of the teeth.

Having brought the base of the ladle to the end of the left side, one should cause the entire clarified butter to reach the fire with a stream measured at two finger-breadths; thus having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sit down and pay homage to the ashes of the fire.
One should fashion a *śruc* (ladle) with a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) made from seven finger-breadths above the base, a neck of one finger-breadth, and a height for the altar of five,
six, or seven finger-breadths, expanded at the top by three finger-breadths; it should have an exit for the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the back of the little finger,
a hollow of three finger-breadths, and five or six circular depressions (*gartamaṇḍala*).
The *śruva* has a handle with a circumference equal to the thumb's width; its hollow at the base of the handle is one *karṣa* in capacity;
it has four ridges at the root and tip of the handle; its bowl (*puṣkara*) is shaped like a cow’s hoofprint;
it is joined with two knobs on its back; and it measures twenty-four or twenty-two finger-breadths in length.
Having taken [the darbha grass], sprinkled it with water using the Astra-mantra, covered it with the Kavaca-mantra, heated it over the fire, and whirled it around,

one should touch its tip with the tip of the darbha, whirl it again, touch its middle with the middle, whirl it again, and touch its root with the root— thus [purifying] the three principles (tattva-traya).

Having placed Śuci and Śakti upon the two *śrucis* and Śambhu upon the *śruva*, one should establish them with their faces downward upon *darbha* grass in the north-eastern direction of the self; then, having worshipped them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
one should bring the clarified butter (*ājya*), sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*, veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*, and [place it] in the Śiva-fire with the *astra-mantra*.
Having heated it with a single utterance of his [mantra], having circumambulated this sacrificial pit three times to the right,
and having set it down, he should take a purifier made of two tips of *darbha* grass joined together, one span in length and knotted in the middle,
grasping it with the thumb and ring finger while facing the fire.
Having performed the threefold sprinkling with the *kavaca* [mantra],
the facing-sprinkling (*saṃmukha-saṃplavana*) with the *hṛdaya* [mantra],

and having cast the *viḍaka* into the fire, one offers the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *astra* [mantra] without looking at it; having performed the purification (*nirājana*), [one worships] in the Śiva-fire.

Having consecrated [the ghee] with the root mantra and rendered it nectar-like by means of the *amṛtamudrā*, and having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should place a *darbha* blade of the length of a span (*prādeśa*) into the center of the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya*).
Then, from the left, one should visualize the three channels (*nāḍī*) named *iḍā*, *suṣumnā*, and *piṅgalā*. [Then recite: *Oṃ agnaye*.
Svāhā! To the left: Oṃ somāya svāhā! From the center: Oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā!

Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā—having offered this oblation with the animal-veni (*paśuveṇa*), one should drop a drop into the unconsecrated ghee for the sake of its consecration. [This applies to] the dark fortnight.
From the left: *oṃ agnaye svāhā*. From the right: *oṃ sūryāya svāhā*. From the center:

*oṃ agniṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*. Then, having performed the three oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the mouths of the fire with the mantra *oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā*, [one should always proceed].

Having unified the faces through their respective mantras by means of the union of the faces— Vāmadeva with the left face, Aghora with the right face, Tatpuruṣa with the Tatpuruṣa face, and Īśāna with the Īśāna-Śiva face— one should fashion the mouth of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to its desired dimensions.

Oṃ, homage to the Vasus. Oṃ, homage to the Ādityas. Oṃ, homage to the Rudras. Oṃ, homage to the Sādhyas. Oṃ, homage to the Nakṣatras. Oṃ, homage to the Earth. Oṃ, homage to those who move upon the Earth. Oṃ, homage to the beings who move in the intermediate space. Oṃ, homage to the Sky.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to the spirits who roam the heavens. Oṃ, homage to the directions.

Oṃ, homage to the spirits who roam the directions. Thus [one offers] to those who are abundant. Having offered a circular water-offering (vali) to the south: Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the source of all beings, the self of all, who is accessible through meditation.
One should offer the *vali* (food offering) with the word "namaḥ" in the center of the maṇḍala. Then, outside the maṇḍala to the south, one should offer: *oṃ barhiḥ pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ*;
*oṃ agniḥ pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ*; *oṃ somapitṛbhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ*; *oṃ*.

Having performed the Vaiśvadeva offering with the mantra, "Svadhā and obeisance to all the ancestors," he goes outside and [offers] to the deities of the directions: "Oṃ, accept this, obeisance to Indra; Oṃ, accept this, obeisance to Aindrī;
Oṃ, accept this, obeisance to Agni; Oṃ, accept this, obeisance to Āgneyī; Oṃ..."
Oṃ, accept this, homage! Oṃ, Yāmyā, accept this, homage! Oṃ, Nairṛta, accept this, homage! Oṃ, Nairṛtī, accept this, homage!
Oṃ, Varuṇa, accept this, homage! Oṃ, Vāruṇī, accept this, homage! Oṃ.
"Oṃ, to Vāyavya, accept this, homage! Oṃ, to Kuvara, accept this, homage! Oṃ, to Nāga, accept this, homage! Oṃ, to Nāgamātṛ, accept this, homage!
With these words, one should offer the *bali* together with perfumes, flowers, and incense. Then [one offers to] the crows and the worms.
"May the dogs, the outcasts, those who have broken their vows, and others receive this;
[I offer it] with salutation. Having said this, he should place the remaining food, accompanied by scents and flowers, upon the ground.
[Thus ends the procedure for daily rites in the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva. || 0 ||
Now, the characteristics of the mudrās: having formed the hands in the shape of a lotus, one should place the two thumbs in the center in the form of the pericarp; this is the Padma-mudrā.
Furthermore, having worshipped that which resides in the fire with the Saṃhāra-mudrā while inhaling...
Having withdrawn [the fire] from the mantra of the fire, having brought it to the *dvādaśānta* and settled it in the heart,

and having dismissed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*), one should sprinkle outside near the pit or upon a mandala the Yoginīs, the Bhīṣaṇas, the Araudras, the Vetālas, and the guardians of the field (*kṣetrarakṣaka*), saying: "Come!"

May those who follow the auspicious path accept [this offering]. May they quickly grant me success at all times through this bali-offering presented by me. With this mantra: *he haḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. Those Rudras whose deeds are fierce, who dwell in fierce abodes, and those who are indeed gentle—[may they accept].

"May some who dwell in gentle places, and the Mothers of fierce form, and even the attendants of the [eight] directions— accepting this offering with pleasure in all things— may they quickly grant us success and protect us constantly from fears. With this mantra, and...

Having offered the *vali* (oblation), washed his hands, and gone into the presence of Śiva, he should worship Him and offer *arghya* for the purpose of dismissal (*visarjana*) in reverse order. Then, having withdrawn the limbs of the [divine] portions according to the previously mentioned method and merged them into the *liṅga*, he should dismiss [the deity] with longing, saying, "Forgive me. This is also to be done on the festival days (*parvan*).

One should perform a special worship. Then, desiring to eat, having completed the midday rites, one should perform the hearth-oblation (*cully-āhuti*), the domestic offering (*gṛha-bali*), and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice for the sake of consecrating the prepared food,
while facing the east.

Therein, having gathered food as the sacrificial substance (*satva*) and sprinkled it with water, one should worship Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, all the gods, and Agni Sviṣṭikṛt, beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with "namas" (obeisance).
Then, having offered oblations ending with "svāhā," one should present the ritual offering (*bali*) to the deities of the site (*vāstu-devatās*). Therein:
On the right upper arm: *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ*. On the left upper arm:
*oṃ adharmāya namaḥ*. On the *kañjinī* vessel for joining the wheels:
*oṃ svarasaparivartanāya namaḥ*. On the water vessels: *oṃ jalāśritāya varuṇāya*.
Homage! At the main door of the house: Oṃ, homage to Mahāvighnarāja. On the grinding stone:
Oṃ, homage to Subhagā. On the mortar: Oṃ, homage to Raudrakoṭarī Girikā. On the pestle:
Oṃ, homage to the great weapon, the beloved of Valabhadra.
On the broom: *Oṃ, obeisance to Mṛtyu, impelled by the gods*. At the head of the bed:
*Oṃ, obeisance to Kāma, the flower-armed one*. Beneath the central pillar:
*Oṃ, obeisance to Skanda, the presiding lord of the planets*. Having thus offered the bali-oblation, [one should perform the rite] in the center of the dwelling.
Having drawn a circular mandala and offered perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should present the bali offering to the Viśvedevas. Therein, [one recites]: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.

If [the ritual] falls from two cubits [of the prescribed distance], one becomes pure again through consecration after having performed a hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapta*) of the deity’s limb-mantra.

The meaning of that [text] is also this: there is no expiation when [the semen] has fallen due to human agency, provided it was done intentionally, was accompanied by gain, and has been completely dispersed; yet, because of the extreme gravity of the sin of breaking [the vow], one must not be negligent regarding the *śalākya* (the probe/penis), which is even more extremely grave than the third mantra.

Because it is capable of eradicating faults such as the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), one should recite this [mantra] three times for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the removal of great transgressions. When the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth have been performed upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and the ritual of worship (*pūjākarma*) has not yet been concluded, [the deity] is not yet dismissed (*avisarjita*).

If negligence occurs toward the Lord of Gods while the rite is being performed with offerings such as flowers, one should withdraw the mantras from the image and offer five hundred oblations into the fire of Aghora; one should also recite [the mantra] five thousand times.
Having touched the implements of the deity with one's foot, one should recite [the mantra] five thousand times. [This applies also] when there is idle chatter during the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).

One who is free from disease should recite [the mantra] one hundred times; one who is diseased should simply recite it. For failing to worship the deity for one day, one should fast for three nights and recite thirty [times] each day.
For failing to worship for a month, there is fasting, bathing, the consumption of *pañcagavya*, recitation, and burnt offerings (*homa*).

It destroys the fault of all types of commingling (*saṃkara*). In that regard, for the commingling of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) due to desire, one should perform the *brahmapañcaka* mantra one hundred times.
However, for the consumption of *nirmālya*, one should perform the *brahmapañcaka* fifty times.

One should repeat [the mantra] a thousand times. Through the yoga of infinite [repetition], one is purified by the initiation of the path of the feet (*padādhvadīkṣā*) even if acting out of desire. The distinctions of *nirmālya* (remnants) are now stated: the property of the deity (*devasva*), the substance of the deity (*devadravya*), the food offering (*naivedya*), that which has been offered (*niveda*), the substance for Caṇḍa (*caṇḍadravya*), and the *nirmālya* itself. Property belonging to the deity, such as a village and so forth, is *devasva*.

Clothing, ornaments, and so forth are *devadravya* (divine property); that which is prepared for the sake of the deity is *naivedya* (food offering), and when it has been offered and relinquished, it is *niveda*. That which is given to Caṇḍa is *caṇḍadravya*;
that which is cast outside is *nirmālya*. Even when the deity has been dismissed, [the offering] remains upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).

The *pavitrika* and other such items do not become *nirmālya*. One should neither smell, nor step over, nor give away, nor sell even the six kinds of *nirmālya*. By giving it away, one becomes a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*);
by eating it, one becomes an outcaste (*mātaṅga*); by stepping over it, there is a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*); and by smelling it, one’s conduct (*vṛtta*) is ruined.
Through touch, one attains womanhood; through improper [handling], a Caṇḍāla; through sale, a Śabara. [This applies to] a Guru, a book, fire, a Yakṣa, a Nāga king, and a Yogin.

The Dharmamudrā has the thumb extended; the Viśvamudrā has the tips of the middle fingers joined together with the hands facing each other, the tips of the [other] fingers slightly curved, the two thumbs tucked inside,
and the eight little fingers interlaced.
By joining the middle and index fingers of both hands, one forms the *dhenu-mudrā* (the cow-mudrā).

By extending and flicking the middle and index fingers of the clenched right hand, one forms the *govṛṣa-mudrā* (the bull-mudrā). [The *vāgīśvarī-mudrā* is formed] by the index finger of the right hand extended toward the palm of the left hand.
The *ḍāmanī* [mudrā] is the *sūryamudrā*, formed by striking [the hands]. The *mahāmudrā* of *Śukra* is formed with both hands extended downward. The *dhenumudrā* is exactly as previously described.
Having formed a hollowed gesture (*añjali*) with both hands, the thumbs should be placed upon the root joints of the ring fingers.
In the *saṃyojana* [mudrā], the two hands are joined with the thumbs raised from clenched fists;
in the *saṃnidhāna*, the thumbs are placed within the palms; in the *niṣṭhurā*, they are joined firmly;
and in the [*saṃnidhāna* variant], the right thumb is rotated while the left thumb is turned inward.

When the two thumbs are joined face-to-face with the palms turned downward, it is the *kālakarṇī* mudrā. When the hands are held facing upward and relaxed, extending from the little fingers to the base and tips of the thumbs, it is the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. It is [performed] with the palms turned upward and relaxed.

The *bhava-mudrā* is formed for the casting of fire and other substances. It consists of joining the right index finger and thumb with the left thumb and middle finger; then, having raised the right thumb, one [places] the fingers of the left hand upon the right hand.
The Liṅga-mudrā is formed by the closing of the fists. || 0 ||
(**********) [In the *Nitāya-siddhāntasārapaddhati*, the description of the mudrās is complete.]

Now, regarding the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*): if [the image] is lost due to its own specific defect, one becomes purified by reciting [mantras] and installing another image. This same procedure should be applied to the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*). Even if it falls from the hand while intact, or if it is handled by one who is uninitiated (*adīkṣita*), [the following applies]: [text missing].
Having bathed [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, one should perform a special worship.
One who remains impure from food remnants (*ucchista*) may, by the grace [of the deity], become pure after touching those of the same class;

he should then recite the name of the Lord of his own class. In the event of contact with one who is impure from food remnants or one who is consecrated for sacrifice (*dikshita*), a Brahmin [should touch] a Kshatriya, a Kshatriya a Vaishya, and a Vaishya a Shudra who is likewise impure from food remnants.

Having touched [a person of] another caste, one should fast for a day and night and then recite the mantra of one's own *jātīśvara* (lord of the caste) together with the mantra of the caste that was touched; a Brāhmaṇa, having touched a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, should fast for three days and recite that same mantra. A Kṣatriya, having touched a Śūdra...

O Lord, one should fast for two days. Having touched these who have not been initiated, one should perform twice what was previously stated. For Kṣatriyas and others, if they touch someone of a lower caste, it is reduced by a quarter; a Vaiśya touching a Brāhmaṇa performs half of that, and a Śūdra performs a quarter. A Śūdra...

In the case of contact with a Kṣatriya, they should perform the penance according to the calculation that it is half [of the previous]. Upon contact with one who has abandoned [his caste], having fasted for three nights, he should recite the mantra of his own clan-lord ten thousand times. In the case of contact with a Caṇḍāla while impure from eating, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance and recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times.
