Or, in the case of contact with those of an excluded (vāhya) caste...
For all those who have been initiated, the Guru [should prepare] a square mandala measuring four cubits, with four doors, fashioned with the four colors, and adorned with a four-petaled lotus;
upon its petals in the east, south, north, and west are Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta.
Having worshipped Īśāna at the pericarp and Śiva within the mandala,

and having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should extract the birth to be purified from the *jātīśa* (lord of the caste) established therein, or from the mandala of one's own *jātīśvara*, by means of the mantra of one's own *jātīśa* ending in *phaṭ*; then, by that same mantra ending in *svāhā*, [one should purify it].

Having cast [the soul] into the Lord of its own *jāti* situated within the mandala, and having likewise extracted it, one should likewise join it to the self of the one to be purified (*śodhya*). Thus, having completed the rite of extracting the *jāti*, one should initiate that person. If the Guru is not present, he himself should initiate his own self. [In the] hexagon, having nourished the Lord of its own *jāti*.

Or, having consumed the leavings of one of the same caste, one should fast and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. A Brāhmaṇa, having consumed the leavings of a Śūdra, should fast for three nights and recite it twenty thousand times. A Brāhmaṇa [having consumed the leavings] of a Vaiśya...

Having eaten [forbidden food], one should fast for three days and recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times. Having eaten the leftovers of others, for the sake of self-purification, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance tenfold.
As for the expiation, one should recite [the mantra] starting from ten up to three hundred times, or simply bathe.
From three hundred up to five hundred [repetitions], one should perform the rite with a bath and a nocturnal meal. On that night,
there is no offering of the remains (*nirmālya*) of Śiva or Sūrya upon the images of the Gaṇas, the Mothers, Gaurī, and so forth.

In another ten instances, the worship of the *liṅga* is performed even at the time of the Guru’s exposition, during the consecration of the *śivakumbha*, when the circumambulation of the deity and the Brahmins has been completed, and upon dismissal; likewise for a mobile *liṅga*, one that is not fixed, one made of clay, one painted,
one made of gems, one made of gold, and any other that has just been consecrated— on these occasions, the fourth [offering] is performed.

The period of ritual efficacy (*karmāvadhi*) does not constitute a defilement regarding discarded offerings (*nirmālya*). There is no fault in using lamps, incense, food, and fragrances during worship, nor even in the case of discarded offerings from a river current.

Regarding the two types of threads—those of a corpse (*śāva*) and those of impurity (*aśauca*)—if they belong to another, one must not consume them; having consumed them, [one must perform purification].

If one has consumed [forbidden food] unintentionally, one should fast for one day and recite the Vāmadeva mantra one thousand times. However, if done intentionally, one should fast for three days and repeat the Vāmadeva mantra three thousand times. This applies to the impurities (*sūtaka* and *śāva*) related to oneself, with the exception of touching a person who is in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaki*).
By whom should it be eaten separately? Otherwise, there would be a constant loss of merit.

Therefore, one who abides in his own duty (*svadharma*), is intent on the performance of rites, possesses knowledge, and is endowed with proper conduct, should not cause a constant loss [of merit] regarding purity and impurity as described in the Sūtras.

If the daily obligatory rites are not performed due to negligence, or if one consumes food from a common kitchen touched by someone in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one must fast for three days; however, if it is done intentionally, that same penance is tripled. This should be understood to apply specifically to the consumption of food from a house affected by birth-impurity or death-impurity (*śāva*).

One must not neglect the daily obligatory rites (*nityānuṣṭhāna*). By failing to perform them, one would become equal to a person in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). At the end of that period of impurity, for as many days as the impurity lasted, one should eat only at night, subsisting on barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), bathing three times a day, and reciting the *Bahurūpagata* mantra three times. One should eat only at that [specific] time.

And in that case, where there is constant loss [of the ritual materials], one should perform the rite for each individual occasion: one should recite the *bahurūpa* mantra three thousand times for three days and fast for three nights. Alternatively, when the fire-rituals, deity-worship, and so forth are deficient, one should recite the *sadyojāta* mantra ten thousand times; or, having fasted and preceded by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one may recite it one hundred times.
One should recite [the mantra]. For the consumption of forbidden food by a *vāma* [practitioner], one hundred [recitations of] the *aghora* [mantra];

for forbidden violence, the *aghora* [mantra] at night; for the emission of semen, the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra]. During the day, it is double [the number]. This applies to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

[The initiation] consists of Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, ending with their respective Lords; it is "with seed" (sabīja) when accompanied by authority (sādhikārā), and "without authority" (niradhikārā) when without seed (nirbīja).
Among these, that which possesses the conduct of the rules (samayācāra) is "with seed," and that is the ritual action (kriyā) for the learned.

It is for those who are indeed capable. The *samaya* [initiation] is preceded by the purification of the bonds (*pāśaśuddhi*) and the conduct of the *samaya*; that which is devoid of the conduct of the *samaya* and so forth is the "seedless" (*nirbīja*) [initiation]. It is for children, the simple-minded, the elderly, the sick, women, and those who enjoy worldly pleasures. — The Teacher.

It is "with authority" (*sādhikārā*) because it pertains to the *sādhakas* in their obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites; it is "without authority" (*niradhikārā*) for the *samayins*, the *putras*, and those initiated without seed (*nirbīja-dīkṣita*), because they have authority only over obligatory rites. Furthermore, that [initiation] is twofold according to its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

It is both endowed with action (*kriyāvatī*) and endowed with knowledge (*jñānavatī*). Among these, that which is preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit and the mandala is "endowed with action.
That which is produced solely through mental activity, without those [external rites], is "endowed with knowledge.
It is performed by an *ācārya* who has received authority through initiation (*dīkṣā*) obtained from the Lord of Will (*icchāmūrti*). And it consists of the re-entry [into the womb] and so forth.
The teacher should be one born in the [proper] region, perfected in learning, conduct, and virtues, and possessed of pure intention;
the disciple likewise should be endowed with virtues such as moral conduct and joined with auspicious qualities like meditation.
In that regard, through the meditation on Śiva, there occurs the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), by virtue of which [the disciple] becomes free from all defects.
From that, there arises the Guru, the Self, and the Infinite; from that, initiation; from that, internal and external awakening;

from that, engagement in what is prescribed and withdrawal from what is forbidden—this is renunciation. It is the longing for the highest good, characterized by qualities such as omniscience; it is the cessation of the state of being a subordinate agent, the nature of which is the exhaustion of all duties, and its manifestation is the stability of [liberation].
The fivefold ritual of counteraction and abandonment consists of destruction, concealment, grace, and so forth;

it is the abiding in one's own pure self. Now, regarding the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*): there, the teacher (*ācārya*), having performed the rites of purification and bathing, having turned back all worldly activities, and having entered the sacrificial hall (*yajña-gṛha*), having performed...

The procedure for the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*): Having performed worship of the Śambhu-vessel, the hymn to Śivā, and the Vardhanikā, and having completed the rite of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the Blessed One, having entered this body, shall grace me— who am endowed with qualities worthy of being accepted.

Having received the permission from the King saying "Do so," and having obtained the authorization from the Blessed One saying "I shall do so," he should place a white *uṣṇīṣa*— consecrated seven times with the root mantra— upon his head. Then,
[he should offer oblations] to the Maṇḍala as the witness of all rites, to the auspicious water-jar (*śivakumbha*) as the protector, and to the fire...
As the locus of the oblation (*homādhikaraṇa*), as that which loosens the bonds of the disciple (*tatpāśaśithilikaraṇa*),
and as the benefactor within one's own self (*svātmanyanugrāhaka*)— thus, even within these five loci, Śiva is indeed [the agent], just as Sadāśiva and the others [are].

Having performed the *japa* for the *bhūtas*, one should perform the *sāraṇā* and *apavāsa*. The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), desiring the supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*), should recite [the mantra] a hundred times at the meal while facing that *liṅga*. For the *liṅgin*s of the *trayīnaṣṭika* [tradition], the lords are Sadyojāta and the others; for the *pāśupata* and *kāpāla* *liṅgin*s, they are likewise [the respective lords].
Having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for eating food from a skull, one should recite the mantra of Īśāna one hundred thousand times.
Having prepared the Jātīśvara-maṇḍala and the Liṅgeśvara-maṇḍala,
by means of the application of depositing and extracting according to the method of the Jātyudvāra, [one performs] the initiation preceded by the door of the Liṅga.

One should perform [the rite]. Having eaten food touched by that very person, one who has performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times. Regarding the Liṅga, however, if it is defiled by the breath and so forth, one should recite ten thousand for Maheśa; half of that for Sūlya; less than that for Tadardha; and for the Laghīyas, one thousand. In this regard, what was stated by the practitioner is as follows:

The expiation for a householder-teacher who is dependent on others is double that for one who is independent. This same rule applies to a practitioner (*vratin*) who is dependent on another; for one who is independent, it is three times the aforementioned amount.
All of this is reduced by one-third for a *putraka*; for a *samayin*, it is half of the *putraka*'s portion.

All this collection of expiations— whether prescribed, omitted, or not mentioned, whether performed through intentional or unintentional acts, and according to the distinctions of sin, obstruction, strength, and age—
should be administered by calculating them as equal, double, half, or a quarter of that amount, in accordance with the specific circumstances.
For one who is unable to maintain [the vow],

the father, preceptor, brother, sister, son, wife, and others must divide [the burden] and perform recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and fasting (*upavāsa*) for the sake of its purification.
[In the Vṛttasārapaddhati composed by the heroic Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva,
the section on the rules for expiation (prāyaścittavidhi) is completed.]

Now, regarding the nature of initiation (*dīkṣā*): it is that ritual action by which the bondage caused by *mala*, *karman*, *māyā*, and so forth is severed, and knowledge is bestowed upon the one to be graced (*anugrāhya*). In this context, the one to be graced is of three kinds: the *vijñānākala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala*. Among these—

The *vijñānākala* is joined with impurity (*mala*) alone; the *pralayākala* is joined with impurity and karma (*karman*); the *sakala* is joined with the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with earth. Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is also twofold:
non-institutional (*anādhikaraṇā*) and institutional (*sādhikaraṇā*). Among these, by the Lord independently of a preceptor (*ācārya*), [the former occurs].

That which is performed through the descent of an exceedingly intense power (*śakti*) in the form of grace according to one's own capacity is *aniradhikaraṇā* (without external support). As for the *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, [it is performed] by the Blessed One residing in the form of the Teacher (*ācārya*), through devotion manifested in the forms of the faces that are mild, milder, intense, and most intense.

Having encapsulated that which was performed by the syllable *nipāta*— which consists of the essence of action (*kriyā*), taste (*rasa*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the nature of bliss (*sukha*)— together with its seed-syllable (*sabīja*),
one should grasp it with the *saṃhāramudrā* and place it within the heart of the disciple.

Having consecrated the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the root mantra, one should give it to the child. Having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations, one should present the offering. Thus, consecrated by this sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), the child becomes fit for worship, fire-offerings, hearing the scriptures, study, and so forth, and attains the state of the Lord (*aiśvara*).
The conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a thousand recitations of the mantras— this is declared to be the *sāmayī* initiation,
which bestows the station of Rudreśa.
[Thus ends the procedure for initiation into the observance (*samayadīkṣāvidhi*) in the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati* composed by the Emperor of Kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva. || 0 ||
Then, having fully worshipped the mantras within the mandalas, the Nirvāṇadīkṣā and other rites should be performed.
In that regard, the mandalas are: Sarvatobhadra, Bhadra, Latāliṅgodbhava, Ardhacandra, Svastika, Yonyākāra, Triprakāra, and Navanābha.

For rites of attraction (*kāmyakarma*), one should fashion [the sacrificial post] in the shape of a bow, resembling a chisel, or like an elephant’s tusk; it may also be distinguished by various forms such as triangular and so forth. All mandalas should be made square, and having prepared the square field for the current day, therein—

Having prepared a pure ground with a surface like the belly of a mirror, one should determine the entry and exit of the shadow of the gnomon situated within the mandala during the conjunctions of Puṣya, Pūṣan, and Maghā; then, having established the east and west, one should draw a line extending from east to west using a level cord.

Having designated the Brahma-spot, one should mark two points of equal interval extending from east to west; then, having fixed the *tattva* cord slightly longer than that at those two eastern and western marks, one should form a fish-figure (*matsya*) in the south.
Having stretched a thread extending from south to north to mark the center, one should then place marks in the cardinal directions at a distance equal to half the measurement of the field; then,
using threads aligned with those marks, one should form four fish-figures (matsyas) in the cardinal directions, moving both clockwise and counter-clockwise.
Having established a square by laying out four lines among them, one should construct all the mandalas.
Therein, having divided the square eightfold and thus created sixty-four squares, one should produce a lotus and a pedestal within the central group of four squares; immediately after that—

In the [central] row, a pathway (vīthī) should be made with half a lotus; immediately following that, in the four directions of the row, one should construct four doors equal in size to the lotuses, and from half the measurement of the doors, one should fashion the neck (kaṇṭha), the throat-base (upakaṇṭha), the cheek (kapola), and the base of the cheek (upakapola). Having thus determined the layout, by rotating the thread from the Brahma-position (brahmasthāna)...

Having made four circles three finger-breadths in diameter in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should contemplate that the mantras beginning with *hṛdaya* (heart), which possess qualities equal to those [circles], are the instruments [of action] for me; thus, one considers oneself to be the independent Lord.
One should perform the act of bestowing grace upon the qualified disciple. Then, having prepared two mandalas and offered a seat of *darbha* grass with the *praṇava*,
one should seat the disciple there with his upper body erect, facing north, with palms joined in reverence, while one remains oneself—
Facing east, he should sprinkle [the disciple] with the water of Śiva using the Astra-mantra; strike him on the head with ashes using the Astra-mantra;

and having drawn three lines each above and below the navel with a blade of Darbha grass empowered by the Astra-mantra, he should perform the ritual of Sakalīkaraṇa (unification with the limbs), sprinkle him with the Astra-mantra, veil him with the Kavaca-mantra, and consecrate him with the Mūla-mantra.

Having bound the eyes with a cloth and led [the disciple] inside, one should have them perform the rite of casting flowers and then show them the Blessed One. Thereafter, having prepared a seat for the *praṇava* upon the southern portion of the mandala and seated [the disciple], one should perform the purification of the body through *dhāraṇā* and the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*.

Having worshipped [the fire] in the hand of Śiva through the mantra, having meditated upon it as having the form of radiant energy, and having placed it upon the head of the disciple while reciting the root mantra, one should perform the anointing of all his limbs. Then, having performed a salutation to Śiva, one should bring the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) near to the left side of oneself.

Having prepared the maṇḍala and offered the seat with the Praṇava, having seated the disciple upon it and performed the oblation of the *sampāta* drops, he should place the root of a *darbha* blade into the palm of the disciple’s hand while reciting the root mantra;
then, joining the tip of the *darbha* to the junction of his own thighs, [he should contemplate] the channels of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and the central nāḍī.

Having visualized that [the disciple's consciousness] has emerged from the body of the disciple and dissolved into one's own channel, three oblations should be offered with the root mantra for the purpose of joining the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Then, the two [mantras] should be employed for the entry in order to seize the consciousness. Following that, the *śivahasta* [is performed].

Having offered one hundred oblations for the propitiation of the root mantra used for stabilization, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with a tenth part of that for the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*), and having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for the sake of expiation, he should uplift the [lower] caste from Śūdras and other castes by means of three oblations.
One should offer three impure oblations for the attainment of the state of the twice-born: *oṃ hyauṃ śivāya svāhā*.
"O Blessed One, may his soul—purified by its source, seed, syllable, and state—become a twice-born.
Having offered three impure oblations for the portion of Rudra, [one says]: "O Blessed One, may his soul become Rudra."

Let it be so. Then, having performed sprinkling and striking with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and having entered the disciple’s body by means of the exhaling breath (*recaka*), one should perform the separation and cutting with the weapon-mantra; then, having drawn that consciousness out by means of the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśa-mudrā*) and brought it to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *dhruva* [mantra].
Having completed [the ritual], one should, with the *saṃhāramudrā* and the inhalation (*pūraka*), cause [the deity] to enter one's own heart;
having made it one with [one's self] through retention (*kumbhaka*), and having abandoned [it] through exhalation (*recaka*) to the deities beginning with Brahmā,
one should establish the eight *dhruva-liṅgas* at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths].
The pedestal (*pīṭha*) is formed by three squares connected to the door at the end of the *vāhuvīṣya*;

above that, the *kaṭha* is formed by three squares, consisting of the omission of one outer line from each of the two squares on the south and north, and one central square; and above that again, it is formed by three squares.
Having laid out the water-course (*jalapaṭṭa*), the neck-creepers (*kaṇṭhavallī*) above it, and all the other *liṅgas*,
one should preserve the corner-cells (*karṇakoṣṭhaka*) for the sake of the creepers;
then, having dissolved the remaining lines between the creeper-*liṅgas*, one should [draw] the walkways (*vīthī*), pedestals (*pīṭha*), and lotuses within the cells that remain above that.
One should fashion the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] when the linga arises from a creeper.
In the square, by means of the fifth thread— the thread of the abandonment of the Sūtras— one should draw a half-moon by rotating the thread situated at the center of the western arm.

Having divided a square field into eight parts and thus produced sixty-four squares, one should establish the outer lines of the three outer squares in each direction within the sixteen squares situated at each corner.
When the three middle lines are erased, even though the corner squares are still present, the fifth [square] manifests itself spontaneously within the svastika.

Having divided the square with four doors into eight parts from the corners, one should establish a cubit at the center and, having set aside a portion equal to half the diagonal, two [projections] should be fashioned like elephant frontal globes, placing a cubit on the central thread.
Having drawn the rotating thread from south to north and leading it to the eastern end, one forms a shape like a *yoni*;
within the two *kumbhas*, the door facing the lotus is in the form of a *yoni*.
In a square divided into three parts, nine lotuses are joined together at their centers, forming nine interconnected naves.

Having divided [the space] fivefold and prepared twenty-five squares, one should establish eight squares connected by horizontal lines in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the ninth square in the center; then,
by omitting sixteen of the remaining squares, the others should be joined together in a continuous pattern.
One should fashion nine lotuses joined together in the *saṃsaktaka* [arrangement]; both of these mandalas are likewise devoid of doors and other such features.

Having divided [the area] into seven parts and produced a path with twenty-four squares— along with one square for the outer border and a quarter-square— consisting of forty-nine squares in total, one should place [the deities] in the remaining twenty-five squares, starting from the east and including the ninth square in each direction.

Having established [the central area] in the middle by means of a sixteen-square grid, one should form four paths; within these, nine lotuses are made unattached to one another, and eight doors following the paths are likewise unattached. Thus, there are three types of the nine-navelled [mandala].

On that square field, having laid thirty-two lines among the *satvis* and the *satvyantaras*, one should form sixteen half-moons by rotating the side-lines outward from the *satvyantara* lines on the third circle; thus, two pairs of half-moons are formed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

In the center, the tips of the petals are on the fourth circle, the joints of the petals are on the third circle, and the tips of the filaments are on the second circle; on the first circle is the yellow pericarp (*karṇikā*) measuring the same as that circle,
in the middle of which are nine blue seeds, white, red, and yellow at their base, middle, and tip respectively.

One should fashion the lotus such that its mass of filaments and petals, together with the pericarp (*prativāraṇā*), are of the color of pure white (*śuklavarṇa*). Its petal-tips should be elevated for one desiring enjoyment (*bhukti*);
straight for one desiring liberation (*mukti*); sharp-tipped for a sacrifice to Smara and other deities; and having the peak of Mount Mandara for [the representation of] the directions and time.

The tip of the *gokarṇa* is for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the planets; the tip of the *maṇḍala* is for the Gaṇas; the *aśvattha* is for the Yantra; and the half of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is for Gaurī, Sarasvatī, and the others.
Outside, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be symmetrical, provided with blue joints and pins.

Having fashioned [the mandala] with white, red, yellow, and black feet and variegated limbs, one should construct the path (vīthī) by means of half a door from the urine-gate (mūtradvāra); then the door-neck (dvārakaṇṭha) extends south and north for that same distance, and the neck-enclosure (upakaṇṭha) for that same distance; half of that is the skull (kapāla), and from there it extends south and north.
First, in front of the mantra,

one should place a human skull externally; having fashioned three lines— white, red, and black— which represent the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, these lines should be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in measure.

In the Sarvatomukha and Bhukti-cakra, all lines should be made equal for one who desires liberation and one who desires enjoyment. Having preserved the lines at the door, the neck, the vicinity of the neck,
the skull, and the vicinity of the skull, one should erase the remaining lines at every corner in the Sarvato-bhadra.
In all mandalas, the lotus doors are not to be constructed in this manner. || 0 ||
This very *sarvatobhadra* becomes a *bhadra* by omitting one square from each of the six squares situated at the corners and from the single square situated in the center. White is produced by chalk;
yellow by turmeric; red by vermilion, red ochre, brick, and the like; and black by burnt barley and so forth.
For the purpose of producing that blue color, one should prepare black powder using charcoal, dry cow-dung, leaves, and so forth;
however, one desiring the attainment of specific accomplishments (siddhi) should perform this very same rite using pearls, coral, and the like.

Having divided a square field into twenty parts in each of the four directions, one should produce four hundred squares; then, having provided a pathway in the outermost row on all sides, one should erase two squares in each row within the next four rows.

One should construct four doors. Having established the doors following the two internal pathways (*vīthī*), one should offer ten *āhuti*s for the sake of purification; then, having resolved upon the removal of impurities and other stains, one should again offer three oblations with the root mantra. Of the ritual action...

Even for one who is pure, having contemplated the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)—that is, the disjunction [of the bonds]—one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) and effect the disjunction of the three bonds of the Lord, which consist of the nature of *māyā*, impurity (*mala*), and karma.
Thus, the disjunction of the three bonds is initiation (*dīkṣā*); it is the severing of the bonds.

Having offered three oblations with the Astra-mantra for the Nivṛtti-pāśa, which consists of impurities (mala) and so forth and pervades the principles (tattva), one should then offer three oblations with the Mūla-mantra, saying:
"O Blessed One, effect the severing of the bonds of Nivṛtti from this self. Upon the destruction of the entire body...

Having contemplated the oneness of consciousness, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra joined by the *vauṣaṭ* syllable. Thereafter, having invoked [Brahman] with "Oṃ, salutation to Brahman" and worshipped him, one should offer three oblations.
Having offered the three oblations with "Oṃ, Brahman, do not accept sound or touch; svāhā,"
One should cause [the disciple] to hear [the teaching] out of compassion, so that he may go to the state free from affliction.

This command of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī) must be entrusted by the wise; having bestowed this command upon Brahmā and the other causal deities, one should dismiss them. Thus, at the summit of the pure reality (tattva)...

Having meditated upon [the self] as being like a pure crystal gem, free from the web of the *nivṛtti-kalā*, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra and perform the extraction: "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, effect the extraction of this [self] from the bond of the *nivṛtti-kalā*. Having thus extracted it, one should proceed.

Having established [the deity] within oneself by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* and the process of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should, upon exhaling (*recaka*), cause it to enter the disciple's body along with the thread. To ensure stability, one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*).
Thereafter, having worshipped Vāgīśvarī and offered three oblations with "Oṃ Vāgīśvaryai Svāhā," [one should proceed].

One should dismiss [the deities]. The conjunction of the *kalās* is twofold, according to the division of pure and impure; the rite should be performed in two forms: having uttered the pure [syllable] short, one should utter the impure long. Having worshipped with "Oṃ hlaṃ hvīṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā," one should offer three oblations.

Having conceived that the pure [consciousness] has dissolved into the impure, one should establish the second digit (*kalā*). First is *Śakti*, then the *Tattva* (Principle), and the manifold nature of *Vāgīśī*. This involves the taking of the disciple’s consciousness, its conjunction with all wombs (*yoni*), as well as [bestowing] the womb, birth, sovereignty, and the attainment of its enjoyments.
One should simultaneously effect the separation from and the removal of the impurities of the womb.

Then, having offered three oblations with the root mantra, and having offered [one] to Śiva with "oṃ hauṃ śivāya," [one should pray]: "oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā! O Blessed One, for this soul, simultaneously bring about [the cessation] of all wombs."

"Perform [it]," he says. Having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the completion of the embryo (*garbha*), he says: "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, effect the completion of the embryo for this self in all wombs, perform, perform! Then, having likewise performed three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of the *caitanya* (consciousness), he says: "Oṃ hauṃ, to Śiva..."
Svāhā! O Blessed One, bring about the generation of this self and of all embryos—do it, do it!

For the sake of the simultaneous growth of all bodies and the accomplishment of their enjoyments, [bestow] that which arises from prior karma and is gathered into one, bestowing fortune upon all bodies of every womb.

Having meditated upon *karmārjuna* and offered three oblations with the root mantra: "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, perform the clearing of karma (*karmārjuna*) which bestows various enjoyments for this self.
In the *lokadharmikī* [rite], one performs the clearing of karma (*karmārjuna*) which consists of the nature of dharma regarding past and future actions.

The offering of the *sambhāvya-āhuti* must be performed; O practitioner, in the initiation (*dīkṣā*), the preliminary rite (*prākkarma*) consisting of the *sambhāvya-udabhidāna* should be carried out. Subsequently, that which is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past and future karma takes various forms according to the distinctions of the body and its objects, resulting in the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
Having contemplated the experience consisting of pleasure and pain within one's own self, three oblations should be offered with the root mantra:
*oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*. This is for the Blessed One, the Self, everywhere.
One should perform the accomplishment of enjoyments by uttering "kurukuru.

Having mentally conceived the enjoyment—which, within the sphere of worldly phenomena, arises from prior and future dharmas and takes various forms according to the distinctions of place, time, body, and object—one should offer oblations. This [enjoyment] is produced solely by the preliminary rite of the initiate's consecration (*sādhaka-dīkṣā*).

Having contemplated enjoyment (*bhoga*) in its various forms according to the distinctions of place, time, body, and object, one should perform the offering of oblations (*āhuti*). Contemplating absorption (*laya*) in the form of supreme bliss within the constituent parts, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra: *Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*.
"O Blessed One, create within yourself a state of supreme and unsurpassed delight toward enjoyments.

Having offered a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra for the sake of purification—namely, for the removal of [the residual impressions of] birth, lifespan, enjoyment, and latent dispositions—one should again offer three oblations with the root-mantra: *oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*.

"O Blessed One, perform the purification of all karma through the atonement of this self— do it, do it! Having contemplated the state of being free from form and devoid of impurity, emerging from the noose of *māyā* due to the absence of enjoyment,
one should offer three root oblations (*mūlāhuti*) and [realize] the state of being a non-enjoyer, for attachment to sense objects is the prison of impurity.

Having offered three oblations with the root mantra, one should perform the severing of the fetters (*pāśaccheda*) by reciting: *Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva; O Blessed One, effect the disjunction of this person’s karma* (2). Then, having offered three oblations with the mantra that pervades the principles of the binding fetters (*pratiṣṭhā-pāśa*), such as impurity (*amala*) and the rest, as well as the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, according to the scripture, it should be performed.
Again, having offered three oblations with the root mantra, and having made the request: "Oṃ hauṃ! To Śiva, svāhā!

O Blessed One, effect the cutting of the bonds (pāśas) for the establishment of this self, perform, perform!", one should contemplate the dissolution of the entire body and its unification with consciousness, as before.

One should offer [the oblation] to the East. Thereafter, having invoked with "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," established [the deity], and worshipped [him], one should offer three oblations; then, having offered three oblations with "Oṃ, to Viṣṇu, accept this full set of eight, svāhā," one should dismiss [the deity] as before.

Having offered three oblations for the purpose of extraction (*uddhāra*), one should perform [the rite] as before for both the body of oneself and the body of the disciple, saying: "Oṃ hauṃ! To Śiva, svāhā! O Blessed One, grant the establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the extraction (*uddhāra*) of this self. Then, having worshipped Vāgīśī, one offers three oblations.

Having offered [the oblation], he should dismiss [the deity]. The joining of the digits (*kalā-sandhāna*) is as before. Having worshipped with "Oṃ Hrīṃ Hraṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā named Pratiṣṭhā," and having offered three oblations, he should establish the Vidyā. Having worshipped with "Oṃ Hrūṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā," and having offered three oblations, [he should perform] its pervasion (*vyāpti*).
One should contemplate: the principles ending with Māyā consist of twenty-nine phonemes, twenty-seven worlds, and twenty words;
and the nature of impurity (mala), action (karman), and Māyā is pervaded by all [of these].
Having invoked, established, and worshipped the inconceivable Mistress of Speech (Vāgīśī), who pervades all wombs (sources of birth),
and having brought her into proximity with three oblations, one should perform for the disciple the rites of sprinkling,
striking, entry, cutting, elevation, and grasping with the Weapon-mantra (astra) upon all wombs using the Bhava-mudrā.
Having performed the conjunction with the *mūla-mantra*, one should offer three oblations: "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva!

O Blessed One, effect the conjunction for this self in all wombs—effect it, effect it! Thus, having performed the rites from conception (*garbhādhāna*) until dissolution (*laya*), one should perform a hundred-fold *homa* with the *śikhā-mantra* during the expiation (*niṣkṛti*).
One should perform [the rite] with: *oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā*. Having again offered three root oblations (*mūlanāhuti*), one should say:

"O Blessed One, through this atonement (*niṣkṛti*) for this self, effect the purification of all karma, effect it! The separation and the cutting of the fetters (*pāśaccheda*) are to be understood as before; the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is likewise. Thereafter, *oṃ*...

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Rudra" (Rudrāya namaḥ) and offered three oblations, and having offered three oblations with "Oṃ, O you who possess the form of Rudra, accept the fragrance, svāhā," he should dismiss [the deity] as before.
Having performed the extraction (uddhāra) established in the self and that which resides therein as previously described, [he should worship] Vāgīśī.
Having worshipped him and offered three oblations, one should dismiss him with the *yojana* mantra.
The severing of the bonds, the offering to the Lord of the Pūrṇācakra, the extraction, the grasping, the unification,
the application to the body of the disciple, the dismissal of Vāgīśī, the contemplation of the pure principles, and then, having worshipped the Kalā, the worship of Śakti once again.

Having invoked with "Oṃ hvīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā," having established [the deity], having worshipped, and having offered three oblations, one should contemplate the pervasion (*vyāpti*). One should contemplate that the triad of impurities (*mala*), consisting of *karma* and *māyā*, which produces the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and the body of enjoyment (*bhoga-śarīra*) and so forth, is [established] by the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*.
Having contemplated that [the universe] is pervaded,

one should then contemplate the path ending with *prakṛti* as pervaded by the fifty-six worlds (*bhuvana*), the twenty-one words (*pada*), the twenty-three phonemes (*varṇa*), and the three mantras, all pervaded by *pratiṣṭhā*. Oṃ.

One should offer three oblations with the mantra "Hauṃ Śivāya Svāhā. Then one should say: "O Blessed One, [reside] in the kalā of Pratiṣṭhā, along with the principles beginning with Māla and those beginning with Tattva; be present here. Thereafter, having established the various forms of Dhvaniryoni from the principle of Prakṛti down to the principle of Āpaḥ, one should invoke Vāgīśī, who pervades this.

Having established [the deity], worshipped it, and brought it into proximity with three oblations, one should perform for the disciple— sprinkling, striking, entry, cutting, attraction, and grasping— as previously described; then,
by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), [one should bring the deity] residing within oneself [into the disciple].

Having bound [the breath] and having drawn it back from the *dvādaśānta*, one should perform the union with the Self—through the *bhavamudrā*—in all wombs (*yoni*) by means of one’s own manifold manifested form.
Then, having offered three oblations with the root mantra, [one recites]: *Oṃ hauṃ vāyatā* [of the Blessed One, of this Self].

Perform the sacrifice in all wombs; perform the *pāśagarbhādhāna*. Having thus applied [the rites] to birth and the other stages, having offered three oblations with the head-mantra (*śiras*) for atonement (*niṣkṛti*), and having again given three oblations with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), [recite]: *oṃ hau śivāya svāhā*.

"O Blessed One, by means of the expiation for this self, effect the purification of all karma. Thinking thus, and conceiving a separation in the form of exiting outside the noose of Māyā due to the absence of enjoyment, one should offer three oblations with the heart-mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā*.
Again, having offered three oblations with the root mantra, saying: "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva;

O Blessed One, effect the separation of this soul from the bond of Māyā," and again having performed the ritual actions for the impurity (*mala*), one should contemplate the separation [of the soul] as being without refuge outside [the body].
Having offered three oblations with the root mantra, one should say: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva!
O Blessed One, effect the disjunction of the impurity-bonds of this self," while contemplating the disjunction of even that purified karma as being ultimately of the nature of absolute non-existence.
Having offered three oblations for the "deposit" (*nidhāna*), and having performed the sprinkling, striking, and other rites upon the disciple,

one should perform the yoga within those wombs. Purification is achieved through the previously mentioned limits by means of three oblations during the stages of conception, birth, its sovereignty, the attainment of its enjoyments, and its dissolution.

One should perform [the rite]. Having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra for atonement (*niṣkṛti*), one should contemplate the disjunction (*viśleṣa*) characterized by the emergence from the bonds (*pāśa*) such as those beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*). Then, having offered three oblations with the root mantra, [one contemplates] that bond beyond tranquility, which is pervasive and consists of impurity (*mala*) and the rest.
Having offered three oblations with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and performed the ritual severance (*viccheda*), one should offer three oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Then, having uttered: "Oṃ hauṃ! Svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, effect the cutting of the bonds (*pāśa*) of this self beyond the Śānti-tattva," one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as before; thereafter—

At the conclusion of the purification of the *kalās*, having established the bond (*pāśa*) of the rules (*samaya*) and the conduct according to the rules (*samayācāra*) within the initiation of non-manifestation (*nirvija-dīkṣā*), one should purify [it]. Having invoked, established, and worshipped [the deities] with "Oṃ, salutation to the hosts of lords of the bonds of rules and conduct according to the rules" (*oṃ samayasamayācāra-pāśādhipatibhyo gaṇebhyo namaḥ*), [one should perform this] with three oblations (*āhuti*).

Having brought [the materials] close and offered one hundred and eight oblations with "Oṃ Hauṃ Śivāya Svāhā," and having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should utter: "O Blessed One, perform the purification of the bonds of this soul's commitments and conduct regarding the observances (samaya-samayācāra-pāśa-śuddhiṃ kuru kuru). Then: "Oṃ Hauṃ Sadāśivāya Namaḥ."
Having thus invoked and worshipped [the deity], and having offered three oblations, one should offer three oblations with the mantra:

*oṃ hauṃ sadāśivāya pūryāṣṭakāṃśaṃ sanaḥ saṃgṛhāṇa svāhā*. Then, as before, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). Following that, with the *oṃ ha oṃ* [mantra] and the exhaling breath (*recaka*), [one should proceed].

Having extracted [the soul] from the bonds beyond peace (śāntyatīta), having made it pure and utterly stainless, and having established it within oneself and within the disciple, one should place a drop of water on the head. Having worshipped Vāgīśī, gratified her, and informed her: "O Blessed One, you have consumed the victim; now depart."

Having contemplated that his own object— the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*)— is dissolved into the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*), he should establish the self-principle (*ātma-tattva*) as far as the principle of illusion (*māyā-tattva*). Having brought it into presence with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the self-principle," he should offer one hundred oblations while uttering the six syllables with "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva."

One should perform oblations for the sake of purifying ritual actions through the absence of defects in procedure. Having thus established the principle of *vidyā* ending with Sadāśiva, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations while reciting [the mantra] in a low voice (*upāṃśu*);
thereby, one is purified from any deficiency in the recitation of the mantra. Thereafter, having established the principle of *śiva* ending with Śakti...

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations through the practice of mental recitation, one is purified of mental impurity. Thereafter, having visualized before him the Power (Śakti) who resides within the paths, pervades all paths, and is the causal form— appearing like a pure gem— and likewise the disciple’s consciousness, [one should perform the rite] with the tuft of hair (śikhā).

Having consecrated the scissors with the *śikhā* mantra, [one performs] the joining of the parts (*kalā-sandhāna*) by means of the *śikhā* [mantra] through division: "Oṃ hrūṃ hyaiṃ, salutation to Vidyā and Śānti. Having thus offered three oblations for the purpose of invoking their presence (*sannidhāna*):
One should establish peace. || 0 ||

Having invoked and established [the deity] with "Oṃ hyaiṃ, obeisance to the digit of Peace (śānti-kalā)," having worshipped her, and having offered three oblations for her presence, one should then perform, as before, the rites of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), striking (tāḍana), cutting (chedana), piercing (vedhana), union (yojana), the womb (garbha), pervasion (vyāpaka), enjoyment (bhoga), and dissolution (laya).

In the section on the rite of pacification (*śāntikalā*), which consists of the performance of pure rites, three oblations should be offered separately everywhere with the root mantra for the *yoga* and other stages. Having performed one hundred oblations with the armor mantra (*kavaca*) during the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), and having subsequently offered three oblations with the root mantra, [one recites]: *oṃ hauṃ*.

Having recited, "Svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, for the expiation of this self, perform the purification from all bonds," one should offer three oblations while contemplating the separation in the form of exiting from the enjoyment of Māyā. Om Hraum Svāhā to Śiva.

"O Blessed One, effect the separation of this [soul] from its own portion; effect it, effect it!"—thus one should utter. In this manner, three oblations should also be offered for the purpose of separating the impurities (*mala*) and karma.
Having offered three oblations with the *astra-mantra* for the severing of the bonds (*pāśa*), and having offered three oblations with the root-mantra (*mūla*), [the final oblation] should be given.

"Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva! O Blessed One, in this teaching, perform the awakening for me, who am the pervader of the primordial principles (tattvas) and so forth; say 'do it, do it'! Then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before, one should invoke and establish [the deity] with "Obeisance to Īśvara."
Having worshipped and offered three oblations to Īśvara with the mantra "Buddhi-ahaṅkārau gṛhāṇa svāhā," he should offer three more oblations and dismiss [the deity] as before. Then,
having released [the soul] from the bonds of peace (śāntipāśa), he should establish it within himself and within that [deity].
With three oblations using the root mantra, one should then worship Vāgīśa, satisfy him with offerings, and dismiss him;

thereafter, one should perform the union of the kalās according to the division of short and long [vowels]. Having worshipped with "Oṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śānti and Śāntyatītā," one should offer three oblations.
One should establish [the mind] in the state beyond tranquility.
Having invoked with "Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śāntyatītā," having established her externally, worshipped her,

and offered three oblations for the sake of her presence (saṃnidhāna), one should contemplate the pervasion (vyāpti). Having conceived of the state of impurity and karma according to the respective principles (tattva), the sixteenfold path ending with Śakti resides within her.

The three letters are the mantras, one word, and the fifteen worlds; these, in the form of the bindu, nāda, śakti, and kalā, are pervaded by the Śāntyatītā [kalā]. Having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of [the deity's] presence, [one worships] Vāgīśī, who is the source of the bindu, nāda, śakti, and kalā, and the all-pervading [power].

Having invoked [the deity], established [the image], and fully worshipped it, one should not disclose the conduct of the *samaya* there to those who have not been initiated into the auspicious *mantra-tantra*. Nor should one write [the teachings] near them. This is the time for the triple purification (*trivireka*) of the initiation of the descending power (*avatarita-śakti-kalā-dīkṣā*).

Or one should worship Śiva and the fire; one should recite [mantras] together with Śiva. Without offering food to the gods, the fire, and the guru, one should not eat. According to one's capacity, one should give gifts to guests and provide food and roots to the poor. One should also throw [food] for dogs, crows, and other such beings.

One should consume food, drink, and so forth from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsabhājana*). On the sacred festival days (*parvan*), one should perform special worship of Śiva and the Guru. One should always serve the teachers (*ācārya*) and others. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days, one should avoid fish, meat, women, oil, and shaving. [One should eat] only at night (*nakta*).

Or one may provide food; one should protect those who are terrified, those fleeing with weapons, those exhausted by travel, the distressed, the sick, those who know the [true] path, and those devoted to the Lord.
[Thus ends the ritual for initiation in the Siddhāntapaddhati composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva. || 0 ||
Then the practitioner, having purified the three kalās beginning with Vṛtti,

should thereafter purify Śāntyatītā. Immediately after, having meditated upon Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the five mantras, he should unite [the soul] with Śāntika by means of the root-mantra and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Oṃ hauṃ! May there be for the self the power of atomization (aṇimā); svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ! May there be for the self the power of magnification (mahimā);

svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ! May there be for the self the power of levitation (laghimā); svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ! May there be for the self the power of irresistible will (prākāmya); svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ!... [text fragment] ... Oṃ hauṃ!
"May mastery over the self be mine, svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ, may sovereignty over the self be mine, svāhā!

Oṃ hauṃ, may the state of being able to fulfill all desires at will within the self be yours, svāhā!"—with these eight oblations, [one performs the rites] beginning with *nivṛtti* using the jars for the qualities and the feet.

Having consecrated the vessel with the *sādhya-mantra* placed upon the *kalās*, and having empowered it one hundred and eight times with that same mantra, they say that one should then bathe [the deity] with the *nivṛtti*, *pratiṣṭhā*, and *vidyā* jars; thereafter, one should again consecrate [him] with the jar of the *śānti-kalā* by means of the *śāntyatītā*. Immediately after, [one should perform the rite] on the right side of the deity.

Having established [the disciple] upon a pedestal fashioned from *śrīparṇī* wood and other materials, having performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having bestowed the office together with the *uṣṇīṣa*, one should recite the mantra of the target and place it into his hand accompanied by flowers and water. Then, having placed [the mantra] in his heart along with the mantra, one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having gratified the mandala-vessel together with the mantra of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), and having worshipped the mantra of the one to be accomplished upon the southern lotus petal of the fire-altar, one who has received permission should perform an eight-limbed prostration to one's own guru and carry out the propitiation of the mantra. Therein, at an auspicious time during a favorable moment, one should proceed.

Then the disciple, having easily obtained [the materials], should bathe, and the preceptor should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other rites. Having re-entered the interior and performed the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), he should cast [the substances] into the fire, beginning with cow-dung and ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering.

Then, having gone outside, washed the *śruk*, *śruva*, and *kartarī* spoons, performed the *ācamana* and *sakalīkaraṇa* rites, and worshipped Śiva, he should thereafter say: "O Blessed One, by your grace, the purification of the paths (*adhva-śuddhi*) for this soul, ending with the cutting of the topknot (*śikhā-cheda*), has been completed; may he go to that supreme abode."
Having caused the *vibhu-mantra* to be heard, he should cause [the disciple] to blow [on the fire]. Having thus prayed, "Now I shall unite the disciple;

O Lord, let the command be given," and being authorized with the words "Do so indeed," he, being greatly delighted, takes the vessel of *argha*, calls the disciple, and proceeds to the place of the fire. There—

As previously described, having performed the sprinkling of the disciple up to the stage of sakalīkaraṇa, and having accomplished the means of sakalīkaraṇa by offering one oblation for each of the sakalīkaraṇa mantras— consisting of the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), and the satiation with mantras (*mantra-tarpaṇa*)— one should unite the consciousness of the disciple within the Self of Śiva.
In that regard, the teachers, having contemplated the vibration (*āspanda*) which is the reality of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), sit upon the seat of the reality of the point (*bindutattva*).
[The powers are] Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Utkrāmaṇī, Ūrdhvagāminī, Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Amṛtā, Śakti, Kalpatanu, Vyāpinī, and Dhyānarūpā.
[The practitioner], whose instruments [of action] extend beyond the *kalās* as "infinite, protectorless, and supportless," whose instruments end at *samanā*,
whose body is filled by the three principles (*tatva*)— the principle of the pure self (*śuddhātmatatva*), *unmanā*, and *Śiva*—
having performed the inhalation and retention (*pūraka-kumbhaka*), joins the tongue to the palate and slightly turns it back.

With his teeth not touching the teeth of his mouth, his body held erect, the preceptor, having joined the disciple’s self within his own self, should contemplate the channels (*nāḍī*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) as unified within the *suṣumnā*; there, having visualized the disciple’s consciousness as resembling pure crystal, he should utter the mantra.

Having abandoned the causal deities such as Brahmā who reside in the heart and other centers, one should unite the disciple’s consciousness with Paramaśiva through the *pūrṇāhuti* and the external *kumbhaka*.
Then [one recites]: *oṃ hūṃ ātman sarvajño bhava svāhā | oṃ hūṃ ātmana tṛptirbhava svāhā | oṃ hūṃ ātmana...*
*Nādi buddho bhava svāhā*. *Oṃ hūṃ ātman svatantrabhava svāhā*.
*Aiṃ hūṃ ātmana luptaśaktirbhava svāhā*. *Oṃ hūṃ ātman anantaśaktirbhava svāhā*. Thus, by means of these six oblations, one should bring about the [six] qualities.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with water from the vessel, one should cause him to hear the eight pledges (*samaya*): one must not engage in disparagement of Maheśvara, his scriptures, the guru, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth; one must not step over the shadow of the *liṅga*; one must not eat the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*);
and one must not consume food touched by a woman in her menses.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with the root mantra using jars containing earth and other elements placed in the west, north, south, east, and intermediate directions, and having dressed him in two white garments,
one should again worship the deity and place a silk cloth upon his right shoulder.

Having offered the seat beginning with Ananta, having established [the deity], having performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and having worshipped, one should offer the royal insignia such as the crown, the left-hand parasol, the sandals, the fly-whisks, the elephant, the horse, the sword, and so forth; as well as the instruments such as the chalk, the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, the *audarbha* grass, the book, the rosary, and so on; and then [bestow] the command.

He should cause [the disciple] to hear: "From this day forward, having understood and examined the initiation, the exposition, and so forth, you must perform them. Then, the Blessed Lady and the Ācāryas should be informed: 'By your grace, may he carry out the authority granted by me without obstacle. Then—
Having performed the preliminary rites, the preceptor should go to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), perform the five-fold ritual acts beginning with *anivṛtti*,
satisfy them with five oblations for each of the five [deities], and offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then,
with a blade of darbha grass held in his right hand, he should [perform the rite] with the five limbs [of the mantra].

One should mark [the body] starting from the little finger up to the thumb. Again, one should prostrate to the Blessed One and ask forgiveness for any transgression. Having done that, he should exercise the authority transmitted through the lineage of gurus; or else, with great [devotion].
Within the interior of the mandala, [he should place] Brāhmaṇas in the east,

Vaiśyas in the south, Śūdras in the west, and all others in the north-east. Having been purified by the initiation (*dīkṣā*), with bodies cleansed, they should for ten or twelve days subsist on cow’s urine according to the injunctions.

Having performed ablutions, having eaten milk-rice, and being devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī while observing the vow of truth, one should consecrate [the king] during the asterisms suitable for consecration, when the moon is in a favorable constellation. Therein, for the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes, it should be done in due order.
Adorned with five, four, three, two, or one hand-measures of dust,
and beautified by five, four, three, or two colors,
there should be a white lotus drawn in the center, thirty-two finger-breadths in length and sixteen finger-breadths in width, which is to be carried [in procession].

Facing the door, it should be provided with all types of dust-removers and a footstool; the exterior should be adorned with painted creepers and foliage at the entrance, and decorated with balls and other ornaments at the corners of the gateway;
the door should be mounted on its respective vehicle or carried from the eastern direction.

One should draw the mandala. Therein, situated within the enclosure, one should draw eight conchs with white powder in the sequence starting from the east: Ānanda, Sunanda, Nandivardhana, Śrīmukha, Vijaya, Tāra, Sutāra, and Ajñāna; and Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sudanta, Puṣpadanta, Jaya, and Vijaya.
One should likewise draw the pitchers (kumbhas) with the labels "East" and "North," white around the perimeter of the mandala,
variegated, equipped with small bells and large bells, and provided with latticed windows made of pearls and gems.
One should teach this in a place with sacrificial fuel, flowers, and *kuśa* water; a location where the world of the Mothers of the Gaṇas is pinned down by many *liṅgas*;

one that is sprinkled by the practitioner; a temple situated toward the south or north; having avoided what is known as a "field" (*kṣetra*) belonging to a deity, for it is there that the mantra of the *preta* is accomplished; and having performed the ritual action, one should conclude the sacrifice facing east.

Having offered a thousand oblations and given the final *pūrṇāhuti*, one should contemplate that the fiery energy (*tejas*) has pervaded the entire site on all sides; then, having fixed stakes empowered by the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*) in those directions and encircled it with a thread over which the Armor-mantra (*varma*) has been recited, one should perform the rite using seeds upon which the seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been recited.

Having drawn line after line and provided protection with *vālī* offerings, having constructed a protective armor-fence (*kavaca-prākāra*), and having offered the *bali*, one should duly offer the mantra into the well-established *liṅga*. Then, possessing the qualities of the vessel and accompanied by friends, one should perform worship and other rites four times a day according to the procedure. Until the field is perfected, one should not abandon it.

Consuming [the substance] obtained from a sacred field (kṣetra) and brought by a qualified companion, one who performs the rite of atonement for transgressions should worship the desired mantra; or else, with all-encompassing devotion toward those [liṅgas] established by sages, Siddhas, and gods— whether they be made of wood, lingas, or self-manifested (svayambhū), and free from conceptual constructions and latent impressions (vāsanā).

Because they are common [to all], there is no confusion among them; therefore, one should worship them by placing one's own mantra upon them along with the sixfold union (*ṣaṭsaṃdhi*). In the case of installed *liṅgas* whose mantras are unknown, one should extract the mantra from the [presiding] deity, install it according to the ritual procedure for installation, and then worship it.
Having placed the *liṅga* or the *prākramātrikā* [in the heart],

having brought it in by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and led it to dissolution at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) by means of exhalation (*recaka*), and having performed the placement of the mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the mantra while grasping the *liṅga* for six months.

O Goddess, one should also perform the worship of Kṣetrapāla, Lokeśa, and the others in the sādhaka’s residence every day at dusk, as well as on the boundaries of the sacred field (kṣetra) and on festival days.
[Thus ends the ritual for the initiation of the practitioner in the *Siddhāntapaddhati*, composed by the great king of kings, Śīlabhojadeva. || 0 ||

Now, the procedure for the Master’s Initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*): For one who has been initiated through the initiation with seed-syllables (*sabījadīkṣā*) and is endowed with learning, ethical discipline, virtues, and proper conduct, one should perform the Master’s Initiation.
Therein, in the northeast of the sacrificial hall, having seated Ananta upon a mandala adorned with a svastika and other symbols;

Having projected the embodied form onto the disciple, performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, and worshipped it, one should prepare five jars— smeared with white sandalwood paste and containing cow-dung balls, *vanamṛd*, earth from the summit of a mountain, earth from a bull’s hump, and white mustard seeds— free from fish-scales, and [recite] the mantra of Earth.
Having performed the peaceful withdrawal of the five elements together with their constituent parts,

one should constantly recite the mantras eight hundred times for each of the deities, beginning from the *Ādhāraśakti* up to the final stage of supreme dissolution (*paramīkaraṇa*), while they are being worshipped.

Having clothed [the disciple] in two very white garments, having drawn the previously mentioned mandala on the southern side of the [main] mandala, and having placed a board made of śrīparṇa wood or fashioned from gold and other materials—
covered with a new white cloth— the teacher should seat the disciple there and perform the rite of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of all the limbs).

Having touched [the image] with mantras, having worshipped it with white flowers according to the rule of colors, having offered the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and having adorned it with ornaments, one should present it to the Blessed One, saying: "By the grace of this preceptor (*ācārya*), may [the deity] become marked. Then, he [the preceptor] should place it again upon the seat.

Having seated [the person], one should present the royal insignia, such as the parasol and so forth. In this very manner, according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the consecration for one desiring sovereignty, for one who has lost their kingdom, for a woman desiring a son, and for one desiring good fortune. And here are the mantras for the conch and other items: Oṃ.

Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the Self of Bliss (Ānandātman). Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the Self of Sunanda (Sunandātman). Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ, salutation to the Self of Nandi (Nandyātman). Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ, salutation to the Self of Nandivardhana (Nandivardhanātman). Oṃ Āṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the Self of Śrīmukha (Śrīmukhātman). Oṃ...
Āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self of victory. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self of Tārā.
Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self of that [Tārā]. These are the mantras of the conch.

Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self that is Subhadra. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self that is Vibhadra. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self that is Sudanta. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self that is Puṣpadanta. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the self that is Jaya.
Oṃ somyā ūṃ, obeisance to the Self of Victory. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the Eastern Self. Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, obeisance to the Northern Self. These are the mantras for the water-pots (kalaśa). || 0 ||
Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ, homage to all jewels. These are the jewel mantras. || 0 ||
Oṃ iṃ ūṃ, salutations again and again to all the seed-syllables whose essence is Indra. This is the seed-mantra (vījamantra).

Oṃ āṃ iṃ ūṃ! Salutations again and again to all medicinal herbs whose essence is Soma. This is the mantra for the herbs. Oṃ āṃ iṃ uṃ! Salutations again and again to all fragrances whose essence is the earth.
The mantra for incense. || 0 ||
Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ! Salutations again and again to all the Mothers, whose essence is the earth.
The mantra for the earth:

Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, obeisance to the gateway of the Lord of the Asuras, whose essence is the Nyagrodha tree. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, obeisance to the gateway of the Lord of Radiance, whose essence is the Palāśa tree. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ...
Oṃ. Salutation to the archway of Dharmarāja, whose essence is the Udumbara tree. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ.
Salutation to the archway of the Lord of Rākṣasas, whose essence is the Siddhaka tree. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ.
Salutation to the archway of the Lord of Waters, whose essence is the Aśvattha tree. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ...

Salutation to the Madhuka-souled gateway of the Lord of the Maruts. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the Pṛkṣa-souled gateway of the Lord of the Yakṣas. Oṃ Āṃ Iṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the Viśva-souled gateway of the Lord of the Vidyādharas. Thus end the mantras for the gateways.
Thus, O Great King of Kings,
one should arrange a canopy adorned with a garland of jewels, provided with fly-whisks, silk ribbons, and fine cloth, and decorated with hanging amulets, balls, and other ornaments.
Within the interior of the mandala, one should create a variegated design using lotus petals covered with a mechanical device in the intermediate spaces,
and on the outside with white rice, broken grains, rice, black sesame,
stalks of dūrvā grass, and powders. And this is its means of crossing over.
Adorned with banners, kusha grass, bark-cloth, and flowers, and provided with a garland for worship,
one should plant a nyagrodha tree in the east, an audumbara in the south, an aśvattha in the west, and a plakṣa in the north, and likewise in the intermediate directions.
And one should place them upon a pedestal made of excellent wood; likewise, the pitchers representing the deities,
their necks marked with svastikas fashioned from yellow orpiment, filled with all kinds of gems and all seeds,
[and accompanied by] Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Viṣṇukrāntā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, and Balā.
With the herbs known as vālā, hemapuṣpī, viṣālā, nākulī, gandhanākulī, sahā, sahadevā, varāhī,
śatāvarī, medā, mahāmedā, ṛddhi, vṛddhi, kākolyā, kṣīrakākolī, jīvaka, and ṛṣabhaka— using whichever of these medicinal plants, fragrances, and roots are available.

One should place [the vessels], filled with garments and garlands, their necks smeared with sandalwood paste, and consecrated a hundred times, outside the *yogapīṭha* in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Therein, [the deities are]:
Ānanda, who is not overly tall; Sunanda; Mahākukṣi; Nandin; Sunābhi; and Nandi.
Vardhana, Hrasvanābhi, Śrīmukha, Nābhimaṇḍala, Vijaya, Sunirghoṣa, Tāra,
Uttarāsvara, and Sutāra— these are the conch shells; and Mandara and Subhadra are the jars.
Kiñcidunnata, Vibhadra, Pṛthulauṣ�ṭha, Sudanta, Hrasvoṣṭha, Puṣpadanta, Āmandhara-grīva, Jaya, Śobhana-grīva, Vijaya, Pūrva, and Uttara—
[these are the deities]. Inside the mandala, there is an udumbara tree covered with a new, unwashed white cloth.

Having arranged a *bhadrāsana* thereon, he should seat the disciple upon it— having performed auspicious rites with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, flutes, lutes, and the chanting of the *svasti*, *puṇyāha*, and Vedic hymns— with his face turned toward the eastern door,
while scattering various seeds from vessels containing the *jātavedas* mantra.

With his faces, he was honored by the Gaṇas who offered their joined palms; and with handfuls of earth— resembling blazing torches— taken from the tips of fish, anthills, mountain peaks, riverbanks, confluences of great rivers, the roots of *vilva* trees accompanied by *kuśa* grass,
crossroads, elephant tusks, cow horns, and solitary trees.

First, having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), then with the powder of *vilva*, lotus filaments, and *priyaṅgu*, then with the decoctions of the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*) and all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*), one should consecrate it by sprinkling it with the jars previously arranged and moved clockwise while contemplating the Śiva-tattva. Then:

Having discarded the bathing garment, [one contemplates] the five worlds as the single Śiva: Rāga and Krodha in Caṇḍa; Jyotis and Saṃvarta in Vidyā; Svarapañcāntaka and Niyata in Kalā; and Ekavīra and Śikheda in Īśvara.

Mahātejas, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Tadbhava, Ekapiṅgākṣa, Īśāna, Bhuvaneśa, and Aṅguṣṭhamātra—these are the eight Lords of the Maṇḍala within Māyā. Thus, there are twenty-seven worlds. There are twenty steps. O Pervasive One, O Pervasive One!
Omniscient and insentient Supreme Lord, supreme and inferior, whose form is light, the presiding authority over all yoga,
the imperishable protector, more secret than the secret— *oṃ*, salutations again and again to the one whose forms are Sadyojāta,
Vāmadeva the secret, Aghora the heart, and Tatpuruṣa the face.
To Īśāna, the head, to Śiva, the source of all—Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose food is meditation.
Thus, there are twenty [mantras] beginning with Vyāpin and ending with Dhyānāhāra.
In this way, the fivefold path is [conjoined] with the sixth, the Vidya-kalā.
The pervasion is indeed the pervading of the sixfold path. || 39 ||
Furthermore, in the Śāntikalā, there are three principles (*tattva*) ending with Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Śiva;
three phonemes, namely *śa*, *kha*, and *ka*; two mantras, Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca;
and eighteen worlds: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, and Balavikaraṇī.

Oṃ, obeisance to Saumyā, the subduer of all beings, the one who brings the mind and self to rest, within Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). Obeisance to the eight worlds: Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Rudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin; [obeisance] to Sadāśiva in the *tattva*.

The world [resides] within the principle of Sadāśiva. Thus, there are eighteen worlds and eleven steps. To the eternal, constant, unconditioned, and infinite Śiva—who is established upon the seat of yoga for the yogin, who is all-pervasive and whose form is space—[one offers worship] eternally with the mantra "Vyomavyāpin."

The eleven words ending with "yogine," "nitya-ādi," and "vyomavyāpine" constitute the fivefold path (pañcavidha-adhvā) pervaded by the Śāntikalā; thus, the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidha-adhvā) is pervaded. Furthermore, within the Śāntyatītā [kalā], there is the Śiva-tattva, consisting of the sixteen vowels as phonemes (varṇas).

The three mantras beginning with the Visarga and ending with the letter *a*—namely *Śiva*, *Īśāna*, and *Astra*—constitute fifteen worlds. The worlds of the *bindu-kalās* are *Nivṛtti*, *Pratiṣṭhā*, *Vidyā*, *Śānti*, and *Śāntyatīta*. [The Yoginīs are] Indikā, Dīpikā, Rovicā, Movicā, and Ūrdhvagā.
The worlds of the *nādakalā* are: Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, Anātha, and Anāśritā;

these are the worlds of the *śaktikalā*. The world of *vyomavyāpi* is the mantra beginning with *ukāra*, which is the single *pada*. The knots of impurity (*malagranthi*) are produced from threads spun by a twice-born girl’s ear-twisted cotton and the like.
Having taken up the *pavitrakas*— which are equal in measure to the width of the *liṅga* or [of the deity] from its full extent— and having sprinkled them with *arghya* water while reciting mantras,
one should [place] that which consists of the *āsana* beginning with the deer-skin (*mṛgājina*) as the witness for all rites, the imperishable Self.

Having performed twenty-one oblations with clarified butter and other substances, accompanied by the *śivamala* mantra, for the purpose of attaining the fruits of ritual action and turning away from worldly existence; having offered perfumes and purifying threads to the Sun; having sipped water four times; having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite; and having prepared the *argha* vessels— [The practitioner should proceed.]

Having offered the fragrant *pavitraka* to Nandin and the others after encircling [the site] with the triple-thread (*trisūtrī*)— [the area] consisting of the *pāśageya*, the bull-station (*vṛṣasthāna*), the temple, the fire-sanctuary, and the wind-gate (*kavāta*)— and having entered as before, one should offer to Vāstoṣpati and Brahmā, saying: "O Blessed One, these have been consecrated."

Having announced, "I offer these to the Blessed One residing in the *kumbha*," and having received them from those who have offered them for that moment, [one places] the *astra-varṇanyāsa*, the *gandha*, and so forth in the *śivakumbha*. [The sequence is]: Śiva, Īśvara, Sthaleśvara—thus the eight worlds (*bhuvanāṣṭaka*), and the *gandha*.
Starting from the level of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) up to the end of the syllable *phaṭ*, situated on the path [of the phonemes],
there is the group of eight deities— Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājeśa, and Brāhma— in the intellect (*buddhi*). Then there are Akṛta, Kṛta, and Bhairava.

The eightfold yoga consists of the Brahma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Auma, Grai, and Kaṇṭha [yogas], located within the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the qualities (guṇas). Thus, by these seven groups of eight, there are fifty-six worlds.
There are twenty-one steps belonging to Maheśvara, the Supreme Self, namely Śarva, Sarva, and Śiva.
O you whose origin and end are the emergence of treasures, who are without end; Oṃ Svaḥ, Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, Oṃ Bhūḥ; Dhū Dhū;

O you who are manifold, beginningless, without ashes, without smoke, without fire, and formless; O you whose splendor is primordial and formless—thus, from the word "Maheśvara" down to the word "formless," these constitute a single [section].
Twenty. Thus, having contemplated the fivefold path as pervaded by the sixth, the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*, the pervasion of the sixfold path is established in this way.

Furthermore, within the *vidyā-kalā*, these principles (*tattvas*) exist: Puruṣa, Rāga, Vidyā, Kalā, Niyati, Kāla, and Māyā; these seven have seven syllables each: *ḷ ṛ ja bha* [etc. as the mantra, one *śikhā*, twenty-seven worlds, and six [deities] in Puruṣa: Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna, and Ekavīra.

The pervasion of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhva*) consists of Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, and that which is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, within the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, there are the four elements: water, fire, air, and ether; as well as smell, taste, and form.
Touch and sound constitute the pentad of subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*).

The organs of action (*karmendriya-pañcaka*) are the mouth, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. The organs of perception (*buddhīndriya-pañcaka*) are the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose. The three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa-traya*) are the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*).

The qualities (guṇas) and primordial nature (prakṛti)—these are the twenty-four principles (tattvas). [The consonants are: ṣa, śa, va, la, ra, ya, ma, bha, va, pha, pa, na, dha, da, tha, ta, ṇa, ḍha, ḍa, ṭha, ṭa. Thus, there are twenty-three letters. The three mantras are the Śiraḥ-mantra, Vāmadeva, and Ghorā. There are fifty-six worlds (bhuvanas).

Amareśa, Prabhasa, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Āṣāḍhi, Diṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhṛti, and Lakulīśa— these are the eight [shrines] in the principle of Ahaṃkāra (Ego). Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpeśvara, Āmrātikeśvara, Amauśvara, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and Bhairava— [these are the eight in the principle of Buddhi].
The eight worlds (*bhuvana*) reside in the principle of fire (*tejastattva*). These eight worlds are Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nakhalaka, Nakhalavimala, Īśvara, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmeśvara.
[Furthermore, there are] the ten million Rudras at Sthāṇupada, Avimukta, Mahālaya, and Gokarṇa.

Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu—these are the eight worlds in the sky (*ākāśa*). Bhū, Galaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, and Kāliñjara. Oṃ, [this is] for Saumyā; ashes from the west with the *sadyojāta* mantra; clay from the north with the *devena* mantra; and the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree.

Water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are for the northeast with the *Īśāna* mantra; the materials for the fire-oblation (*homadravya*) and the *kuśa* grass are for the east with the *Sadyojāta* mantra.

With the [mantra] beginning with *yena yām*... the staff, rosary, loincloth, and alms-bowl are for the south with the *Aghora* mantra; the yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), saffron, oil, and the probe (*śalākā*) are for the southeast.
One should offer another *sādhana* with the *Aghora* mantra, or with the *Vāmadeva* mantra for the north;

with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra, one should place betel-leaf and cooked rice in the east; and with the *Īśāna* mantra, one should arrange the seat, sandals, umbrella, and sacrificial implements in the northeast. Whatever among these has been prepared [should be offered].

One should mentally visualize that.
