Then, having sprinkled the moving offerings (caru) belonging to Śiva with the Astra-mantra, veiled them with the Kavaca-mantra, worshipped them with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and turned them into nectar with the Dhenu-mudrā, one should offer them to the Blessed One with the Brahma-mantras. Then, [the offering] from the size of one hand up to nine hands...

Regarding the lingas, a nine-threaded cord is fashioned starting from twenty-eight threads and increasing by ten up to one hundred and eight, according to the size of the linga; this applies to those made of jewels as well. For other lingas, they may be fashioned otherwise according to one's capacity, either as one hundred and eight or with eighty-one threads.
The threads, colored with saffron and other pigments, are fashioned in lengths of fifty, thirty-eight, or thirty-six;
this is the procedure for the initiation of the teacher according to the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati* composed by Śrī Bhojadeva.

Now, the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) pertaining to initiation is its pervasion (*vyāpti*): therein, the earth principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*),

the letter *kṣa*, the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), the Sadyojāta-mantra, and the six worlds within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)— namely Kālāgni, Kuṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— as well as those outside.

The eleven Rudras, beginning with Śatarudra, are stationed in the directions. In the eastern quarter, there are ten: Kapālīśa, Aja, Vuddha, Vajradeha, Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śānta, Apinākin, and Tridaśādhipa. [In the southeast: Agnirudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, and Hara.
Jvalanodahana, Ugrabhru, Bhasmāntaka, Kṛpāntaka—thus ends the tenth [chapter] in the Āgneya-purāṇa.
The Destroyer, the Increaser, the Ordainer, the Non-Ordainer, the Doer, the Uniter, the Separator,
the One who possesses both Dharma and Adharma— thus is he tenfold. The Toothless, the Killer, the Slayer,
the One of Cruel Gaze, the Terrifying, the One with Upturned Abode, the Odd-Eyed, the Smoky, and the Red.

"Daṃṣṭravān" and so forth—these ten are in the southwest (Nairṛta). "Bala," "Atibala," "Pāśahasta," "Mahābala," "Citra," "Jayabhadra," "Dīrghabhadra," "Oṃ," "Meghanāda," and "Sunāda"—these ten are in the west (Vāruṇa).

Śrīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, Akṣaya, Antaka, Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghanāda—these are the ten [names]. Oṃ! To Saumyā, whose form is beautiful, who is auspicious, whose body is gentle, who bears matted locks, and who is the bearer of Lakṣmī.

In the north [are] ten: Ratnadhara, Śrīdhara, Prāsāda, and Prakāśa. In the northeast [are] ten: Vidyādhipa, Īśa, Sarvajña, Jñānadṛk, Vedapāda, Sureśa, Sarvajyeṣṭhabhūta, Pālavali, Priyā, and Vṛṣaparānantakrodhanamārutāsanagrasana.
The ten below are Udumbarī, Śaphaṇīndra, Vajrī, Daṃṣṭrī, and so forth;
the ten above are Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tridaśa, Tridaśeśvara, Sambāha, Vivāha, Nabhalipsu, and Trilocana. Of these, Virabhadra and Bhadrakālī are at the head.

The two worlds—thus, one hundred and eight worlds; salutations again and again! Oṃ, salutations, salutations to Śiva! O Sarva, Śiva, Sūkṣma, Śabda, Jñāna, Piṅga, Turu, Pataṅga, Sākṣin, Pūrvasthita, Astuta, Astuta, Arcita, Anarcita!

O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, O you who bring about the prosperity of all, O source of existence who bestows happiness upon all beings, O Bhava, O Lord of all Pramathas, release me from the affliction of yoga, O you of great splendor! Svāhā! O Great God, Lord of true being! Thus [it is said].
The twenty-eight words beginning from the end of the *vyomavyāpin* mantra down to the word *mahādeva* constitute this fivefold path (*adhvapañcaka*), which is pervaded by the sixth [tattva],
the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
Homage to Māyā. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgāra. Oṃ, homage to Budha. Oṃ, homage to Bṛhaspati.
Oṃ, homage to Śukra. Oṃ, homage to Śanaiścara. Oṃ, homage to Rāhu. Oṃ, homage to Ketu. Thus, [the offerings] with Svāhā. Oṃ, vaṣaṭ, homage to all beings. Thus.

The elements (*bhūtāni*). Then, having performed the *avasavya* (counter-clockwise) motion, and having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing southward, [he sprinkles] water mixed with sesame seeds while reciting: "Oṃ, Soma, Agni, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mānya, Aṅgirasvān, Agni..."
I satiate with *svadhā* those ancestors, Kavyavāhana and the others; *oṃ*, I satiate with *svadhā* the wives of the ancestors; *oṃ*, I satiate with *svadhā* the hosts of ancestors;
*oṃ*, I satiate with *svadhā* the hosts of the wives of the ancestors. Then, by means of their names and lineages: *oṃ*.

I satisfy my fathers and grandfathers with *svadhā*. Oṃ, I satisfy the great grandfather with *svadhā*. Oṃ, I satisfy the great great-grandfather with *svadhā*. Oṃ, I satisfy the mothers with *svadhā*. Oṃ, I satisfy the grandmothers with *svadhā*.

Oṃ, I satiate the paternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and *namaḥ*. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and *namaḥ*. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and *namaḥ*. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal great-great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and *namaḥ*. Oṃ, [I satiate] the maternal grandmothers...

Svadhā! I satiate [the ancestors]. Oṃ! I satiate my mother’s grandmothers with svadhā. Oṃ! I satiate my mother’s great-grandmothers with svadhā. In this manner, one should also fully satiate the paternal relatives and kinsmen.
Having rinsed the mouth, performed the sakalīkaraṇa, and taken up the general arghya vessel consecrated with mantras in his hand,

he should worship Nandin and the other deities; then, entering within, he should worship Śiva according to the daily rite (nityavidhi), perform the ritual in the fire up to the libation of mantras (mantratarpaṇa), and offer the oblation (aliṃ).

Having offered the mantras to the fire, withdrawing them, and having united them with the Blessed One who is established in yoga, one should dismiss him with the words "forgive me" while maintaining a sense of dependence; thus, having performed the daily worship, one should commence the occasional (naimittika) rite.
Therein, having examined and taken possession of the ground, one should worship the Sun and, whether having dismissed him or not, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having made himself a vessel for the removal of sins, he should proceed to the yoga-maṇḍapa. There,

having sprinkled the doors with the Astra-mantra, he should worship the eastern door with "Oṃ, obeisance to the door of the Śānti-kalā," the southern door with "Oṃ, obeisance to the door of the Vidyā-kalā," and [the western door] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the door of the Nivṛtti-kalā."

For the western [door]: Oṃ, having paid homage to Pratiṣṭhākalādvāra and worshipped it, one should worship Nandi, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, Vināyaka, Vṛṣa, Skanda, Devī, and Caṇḍa at their respective branches, beginning from the eastern door, using their own names preceded by Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Having worshipped with the *nādāstramudrā*, one should cast flowers into the house of Yoga.
The path of the bound soul (*paśu*) is pervaded by the power beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītakalā*);
thus is the pervasion of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvavyāpti*). Such is this sixfold path here.

Regarding the enumeration: therein, the *kalās* are five, the *tattvas* thirty-six, the phonemes (*varṇas*) fifty, the mantras eleven, the worlds (*bhuvanas*) two hundred and twenty-four, and the words (*padāni*) eighty-one; one who is endowed with knowledge of these six paths is said to be liberated from the bondage of existence.
And he causes [them] to be liberated. || 0 ||
[Thus ends the determination of the sixfold path in the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati* composed by the illustrious Bhojadeva, the supreme king of kings. || 0 ||
Now, for the purpose of filling all deficiencies, the procedure for the *pavitra* (sacred thread) is described.
Therein, in any one of the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada, on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of either the bright or dark fortnight, having performed purification—

Having performed the prescribed rite of bathing, one who maintains the sacred fire (*saṃnyāupāsana*) should offer libations. Therein, having made an internal connection, one should satisfy the deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and others—with the *sūla-mantra* and other mantras using the tips of the fingers, ending with "svāhā" and the *hṛdaya-mantra*: "Oṃ vāgvādini svāhā."
(*1) Oṃ, obeisance to Aindrāṇī; oṃ, obeisance to Āgneyī; oṃ, obeisance to Yāmyā;
oṃ, obeisance to Nairṛtī; oṃ, obeisance to Vāruṇī; oṃ, obeisance to Vāyavī;
oṃ, obeisance to Saumyā; oṃ, obeisance to Īśānī; oṃ, obeisance to Nāgadhṛṣṭhā. Oṃ.

Salutation to Nāgabhāgā. Thus for the directions. Oṃ, salutation to Indra; Oṃ, salutation to Agni; Oṃ, salutation to Yama; Oṃ, salutation to Nirṛti; Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa; Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu; Oṃ, salutation to Soma; Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna; Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā; Oṃ...
*Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta.* Thus [having honored] the lords of the directions, then, with the sacred thread over the neck, at the joints of the fingers:
*Oṃ, I satiate Atri; obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate Viśvāmitra;
obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate Dhūmra; obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate Kratu; obeisance.* *Oṃ...*
I satisfy Vasiṣṭha; obeisance. Oṃ, I satisfy Marīci; obeisance. Thus for the ṛṣis.
Oṃ, I satisfy Manaka; obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Candramana. Thus for the Siddhas. Oṃ, obeisance to Āditya; having worshipped Soma...

Having adorned both [the deity and the practitioner] with a pair of white garments, [one should worship] then in the east: *oṃ indrāya namaḥ* | *oṃ vajrāya namaḥ* | *oṃ agnaye namaḥ* | *oṃ śaktaye namaḥ* | *oṃ yamāya namaḥ* (?
| *oṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ* | *oṃ niritaye namaḥ* | *oṃ khaḍgāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa. Oṃ, salutation to the noose. Oṃ, salutation to Vāyu. Oṃ, salutation to the banner. Oṃ, salutation to Kuvera. Oṃ, salutation to [the deity] (***). Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Oṃ, salutation to the trident. [In the eight directions. In that very place: Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā. Oṃ...

Salutation to Padmā. Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, salutation to the Discus (Cakra). In the south-west (Nairṛtya). Having thus worshipped the world-protectors (Lokapālas) together with their weapons on the inner wall-section of the pavilion, [he says]:
"O Śakra, for the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction, you must remain vigilant."
"By this sequence— 'one must remain until the end of the yoga by the command of Śiva'—
proclaiming the command of Śiva to all the world-protectors while recollecting the weapon-fortress (astradurga), [he should circumambulate] the inner wall of the pavilion."
Having circled the *kumbha* together with the *vardhanī* by means of a continuous stream,

and having brought them back to their respective places, one should again worship the stable seat (*sthirāsana*), place both the *vardhanī* and the *kumbha* there, and worship [the deity] residing within the *kumbha*.

One should offer the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) to the Blessed One. Having performed the recitation for the *nirodhārgha*— thinking, "O Blessed One, you must remain here until the sacrifice is completed"— and having offered the *argha* water for the purpose of binding it with that blade of *darbha*, one should leave that vessel stationary right there.
Having established [the deity] with this water from the *vardhanī* vessel,

one should scatter [flowers] and contemplate the sacrificial hall as entirely cleared of all obstacles on every side; thus, having performed the ritual of seizing the ground (*bhūparigraha*), one should approach the presence of the Deity, sit upon one's own seat, and perform the rites beginning with the worship of the seat (*āsanapūjā*) up to the prostration (*praṇāma*).

Having performed the ritual actions and offered water for honor (*argha*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should commence the ceremonial bath (*snāpana*). Therein, having first removed the flowers with the *astra-mantra*,

having brought the jars (*gaḍḍuka*), and having inspected, sprinkled, struck, and purified them with the *astra-mantra*, one should [invoke] the sacred water of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*) into the vessels containing the bathing water.

Having consecrated the water repeatedly with the *pavitra* [mantra] and the *saṃhitā-mantra* while reciting the *saṃkalpa*, and having washed the cloth for the *gaḍuka* with the *astra-mantra*, one should fill it with the strained water using either the *gāyatrī* or the *hṛdaya-mantra* accompanied by the *astravardhanī*; then, having offered a single flower into each [vessel].

Having sprinkled a drop from the *arghya* water, one should bathe the deity with those [waters] while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, having prepared milk, curd, and ghee as the essence of one's particular wealth,
one should [ward off] terrestrial [spirits] by striking the ground three times with the heels.
Having dispelled the intermediate obstacles with three claps of the hands and the celestial obstacles with three *koṭis* [of mantras], and having cast an *udumbara* flower with the *astra-mantra*,
one should enter within by the western door while touching it with the right foot.

Having entered the threshold while reciting the Astra-mantra and having scattered flowers, and having offered a flower at the Brahma-sthāna with the mantra "Obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of the Dwelling," one should protect the sacrificial hall by means of the enclosure of the Astra-mantra and the veiling rite (avaguṇṭhana).

Seated upon the altar facing north, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the ritual of making the *sūlī*, he prepares the vessel for the water of oblation (*arghyapātra*) with mustard seeds, rice, sesame, *kuśa* grass, flowers, milk, and water; then,
having sprinkled the sacrificial implements with that water using *kuśa* grass while reciting "Thou art the edge" (*aśrir asi*), [he purifies] the materials of the sacrifice.

Having sprinkled the collection of substances such as flowers with the *śuddhi* mantra and having sprinkled them again with the *kavaca* mantra, one should consecrate each one individually with the *hṛdaya* mantra. Then, having applied a *tilaka* with sandalwood paste and having placed the *mantrasaṃhitā* upon one's head while performing worship, one should take hold [of the materials] with the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*) as prescribed.
Alternatively, having prepared a sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) consecrated with mantras and fashioned from thirty *darbha* blades,
one should place milk in the central square of the nine-square grid— within the squares representing the *śivatattva*— using the root mantra or the Īśāna mantra.
In the eastern *sadāśiva* principle-square, [one should offer] clarified butter in the form of light twice, with either the *śānti* or the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.

In the southern *vidyā* principle-square, [one should offer] clarified butter in the form of light three times, with either the *śikhā* or the *aghora* mantra. In the northern *puruṣa* principle-square...
In the water-vessel [representing] *ratna*, one should pour cow’s urine with the *Śiras* mantra or the *Vāmadeva* mantra four times;

in the western square [representing] the *Tattva* of *Amṛta*, one should pour cow dung five times with the *Hṛdaya* mantra or the *Sadyojāta* mantra; and the *kuśa*-water should be consecrated six times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
One should place curd and other substances into a well-established vessel;

thus it is prescribed that one should consecrate the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the scattered offerings (*avakirana*). Then, standing in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), facing the northeast (*īśāna*), one should perform the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), moistening (*abhyukṣaṇa*), digging (*khanana*), and scattering (*avakiraṇa*).

Having consecrated the pavilion with the rites ending in filling, leveling, sprinkling, fumigating, sweeping, smearing, and making it adamantine (vajrīkaraṇa), each accompanied by its own respective mantra, and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should scatter the ritual offerings (vikirān) while visualizing them as blazing weapons.

Then, having gathered [the materials] again with a bunch of *darbha* grass and placed them on the altar in the northeast corner, one should bring a pitcher made of gold or another such metal, fill it with filtered water,
and having provided a movable seat upon the collected ritual implements, [one should place] the form of the deity there with the *mūrti-mantra*.

Having placed the *kumbha* (vessel) upon this [altar] and worshipped the Blessed One together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), one should likewise place the *vardhanī* (overflow vessel) to its right; having consecrated it as the weapon (*astra*) through the recitation of the weapon-mantra, one should [light] sixteen-finger-long fuel-sticks smeared with ghee in that [fire], using twigs from the tips and roots of the *astra*-tree.

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) with five or twenty-four oblations using the root mantra for the sake of the naming ceremony, and having offered oblations with the *Īśāna* mantra, one should give the name "Śivāgni" or "Hutāśana" using the root mantra, worship [the fire], and perform the dismissal of the parents.
If, out of negligence, [the fire] has been extinguished by a worldly fire, one should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth,

and having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), one should offer five thousand oblations with the third mantra. If Śiva has been summoned, having likewise performed the consecration and fasted for three nights, one should offer ten thousand oblations to Aghora.
Then one should offer oblations; having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons upon the girdles,
and having worshipped Brahmā in the east, Rudra in the south, Viṣṇu in the west, and Īśvara in the north upon the sacrificial enclosures and seats, one should touch the Śruta and Aśruta [fires].

Having assigned the three principles— the Śakti to the *śruca* and Śiva to the *śruva*— and having placed both [utensils] face-down upon *darbha* grass to the left side of oneself, one should worship them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Then, having brought the elements [of the utensils], sprinkled them with the *astra-mantra*, and shielded them with the *kavaca-mantra*, [one should place them] in the Śiva-fire with the *astra-mantra*.

Having heated it with the armor-mantra (kavaca) and placed it upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should rotate it three times clockwise around the navel and then establish it there, having fashioned from two tips of *darbha* grass a ring one span (*prādeśa*) in length with a knot in the middle.

Having taken the *pavitraka* with the thumb and ring finger, one should perform three splashes of clarified butter (*ājya*) toward the fire with the *Kavaca* mantra, and likewise three splashes toward oneself with the *Hṛdaya* mantra; then, having cast the *pavitraka* into the fire, one should illuminate the clarified butter with the *Astra* mantra and gaze upon it.

One should cast the *nīrājana* (lustration) firebrand into the *śiva-agni*. Then, having sprinkled the clarified butter (*ājya*) with water, consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and rendered it nectarine by means of the root mantra and the *amṛtamudrā*, one should worship it with the root mantra. In the center of the vessel for the clarified butter, [one should place] a *darbha* blade measuring a span (*prādeśa*).
Having placed and visualized the triad of channels known as Iḍā, Suṣumnā, and Piṅgalā, [one offers oblations]: from the right side, *oṃ agnaye svāhā*; from the left side, *oṃ somāya svāhā*;
from the middle, *oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*; and *oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā*.
Thus we offer oblations.

Having bathed the headless base with honey and sugar, interspersed with water and incense, using the root mantra everywhere, and having dried it, one should then [bathe it] with plain water according to one's capacity.

Having bathed [the deity] again with scented water, one should worship Śiva together with his limbs (the retinue) upon a seat in the mandala or elsewhere. Then, having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should go near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). There, one should inspect the pit with the Śiva-mantra, sprinkle it with the *śiva*-mantra, and wash it with the *astra*-mantra.

Striking with the *kavaca* [mantra], scraping with the *astra* [mantra], sprinkling, filling, and pouring; sweeping with a broom, smearing, preparing the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), laying down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the grass seats (*viṣṭara*), and worshipping the pit;
[drawing] three lines extending eastward or northward, together with a transverse line.

Having performed the fourfold *yavajīkaraṇa* and the placement at the crossroads (*catuṣpathanyāsa*) with the sword-mantra (*khaḍgamantrena*), and having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī in her menses and Vāgīśvara as being possessed of desire, having invoked them, worshipped them with the *dhruva*-mantra, and applied the eye-ointment with the weapon-mantra (*astreṇa*) from the fire-drill (*araṇi*).
Having brought fire from a sun-crystal, from the house of a twice-born, from the house of a Vaiśya, or from one's own house,
having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), having sprinkled it with the water from the arghya vessel,
having veiled it with the Kavaca mantra, and having placed the seed-syllable of fire, *oṃ rauṃ*, [one should worship] with the six-limbed mantra of fire.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* while performing the *prāsāda* [mantra] and the *dhenu-mudrā*, thereby transforming it into nectar (*amṛta*),
and having worshipped it, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times. Then, kneeling upon the ground, one should [visualize] Vāgīśvarī facing oneself.

Having cast [the seed] into the womb-duct and offered a drop of water, and having covered it with a cloth for the sake of protecting the embryo, one should tie a darbha-grass amulet consecrated with the Astra-mantra onto the hand of the Goddess;
then, having worshipped with the Sadyojāta-mantra for the purpose of the conception (*garbhādhāna*), one should offer three oblations with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
For the sake of *puṃsavana*, having worshipped with the *vāmadeva* mantra and offered three oblations from the head; then,
for the occasion of *sīmantonnayana*, having worshipped with the *aghora* mantra and offered three oblations from the tuft of hair (*śikhā*),
one should perform the fashioning of the face and limbs and the expiation using the *darbha* grass from that very tuft.

Having worshipped with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra and offered three oblations with the *kavaca* mantra for the sake of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), and having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water from the *argha* vessel upon the child’s birth to remove the impurity (*sūtaka*), one should spread darbha grass around the pit with their tips pointing east and north using the *astra* mantra for the protection of the fire, and then [offer] three oblations.

Opening the mouths [of the deities] for the removal of vomit and saliva, and for the sake of nourishment, one should cook the *caru* with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and the short *prāsāda*-mantra. Then, once it is prepared, one should offer it while reciting the mantra from the *Saṃhitā* ending in *svāhā*, saying: "O well-nourished one, become thoroughly moistened," and having performed the fierce rite upon the heated [substance].

When the second maṇḍala in the Śādika has been fully worshipped, having caused [the deity] to descend with the mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* joined with the mantra, one should make the terrible [heat] cool by saying, "Be cool. Then,
having thoroughly mixed [the substance] from all sides with the mantra-conjunction beginning with *ava* and *yāta*, [one should proceed].
Having wiped the surface with earth and water, and having consecrated it as nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *amṛta-mudrā*, one should lead [the deity] near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Having placed [it] upon a mandala worshipped as before in the western direction, one should worship it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*). Then, one should worship it individually with the limbs (*aṅga*) and with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) one hundred and eight times.

Having recited the mantra ending with "svāhā" a hundred times and poured clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire with the *śruva* ladle, he performs the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Having offered the remainder as a *parihoma*, he should perform the *saṃpāta-homa*—the offering of the residual drops—into the *caru* with the formula "unto the Buddhas. Then, having divided that [caru] into three parts:

Having prepared the portion for Śiva and the portion for Agni, combined with ghee and honey, one should place it [in the vessel] and perform the *saṃskāra* with ghee alone. Then, having worshipped the portion for Śiva with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*,
taken it, and approached the fire, one should worship the Deity and address Him with the *Tatpuruṣa-mantra*.

Having gone to the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and sat down with the mantra, one should offer the scented purifier (*gandhapavitraka*) in sequence to one's own form and to the teacher and the *daṅka*; it should consist of a single knot, made of fine thread, and be consecrated.

Having offered the *pavitraka* together with flowers by means of the mantra, having rendered it nectar-like through the *recaka* breath-retention using the *mūka-mantra*, and having placed it upon Śiva with the *samāropa-mantra*, one should [recite] the mantra consisting of "that which is the self," "the end of sin," "all deficiencies in the ritual," and "the Guru is Śiva. Then...
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and announced it to the deity as before, having prostrated, praised, and asked for forgiveness,

one should offer the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*) to the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*) and the [deities of the] weapons (*astra*) stationed on the inner walls of the pavilion, and then to the Blessed One seated in the fire outside, for the third time.
Having offered to Śaṃkara, one should give the *pavitraka* while addressing him. Then: *oṃ ityādyapratigṛhṇa namaḥ*;
*oṃ agnaye dhurugṛhṇa namaḥ*; *oṃ yamāya pratigṛhṇa namaḥ*;
*oṃ nirṛtaye pratigṛhṇa namaḥ*; *oṃ varuṇāya pratigṛhṇa namaḥ*; *oṃ vāyave*.
"Accept, obeisance!

Having offered the fourfold [oblation] with the *śruva* ladle into the unrefined clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), one should drop a drop for the purpose of recollection. For the dark fortnight, from the left: "Oṃ, svāhā to Agni. To the right... [text fragment].
*svāhā* to Sūrya; from the center, *svāhā* to Agni and Sūrya;

*oṃ* *svāhā* to Agni Sviṣṭikṛt. Then, having performed the three oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) into the mouths of the fires with their respective mantras—Sadyojāta with the Sadyomantra, Vāmadeva with the Vāmamantra, Aghora with the Aghoramantra, and Tatpuruṣa with the Tatpuruṣamantra.

Having performed the joining of the faces with their respective mantras— saying "the Tatpuruṣa face with Īśāna" and "the remaining [faces] with Śiva"— and having fashioned the mouth according to the desired measurement of the *kuṇḍa*,
one should perform the rites from the middle tongue up to the tip of the *cūta* (mango) leaf for the purpose of completing the consecrations.
Having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,

and having established a connection between the two mouths of the fire for the sake of the sacrificial food (*caru*), incense, and lamps, one should recite the root mantra; [the offering] then emerges from the nostril of Śiva residing within the fire.

One should meditate on [the deity] who resides in the flame of the form of light (*jyotīrūpaśikhā*), merged within the crest of Śiva (*śivaśikhālīnā*), whose rays are known through non-separation, who is delimited by that [non-separation], and who has established her abode in both [places]. Having performed the concentration (*sadhāna*) residing in the fire, and having performed the installation (*sāsana*).

Having performed the worship [of the vessel], one should proceed. Then, having washed with water and the *astra-mantra* a vessel made of either metal or clay that is free from defects, having veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*,
having sprinkled it with the *prokṣaṇa* [mantras], having smeared it with [unguents] and perfumed it with incense, [one should place] the *kuśa*-grass bundle...

Having wrapped [the vessel] around the neck with the armor-mantra, smeared it with cow dung on a consecrated mandala, sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra, and enveloped it with the armor-mantra; having placed darbha grass arranged with the weapon-mantra upon a seat formed by six lines and worshipped it, one should place the vessel as the manifested form and worship the Blessed One together with his limbs.
Having removed the flowers and other offerings, one should anoint the vessel with clarified butter and fill it with cow’s milk strained through a cloth.
Then, having drawn lines on the southern, eastern, and western sides with the Astra-mantra, one should sprinkle the vessel with that same mantra and envelop it with the Kavaca-mantra.

Having swept and smeared [the area], and having prepared the remainder for those who partake of dharma and adharma, one should join it with the previously extracted auspicious fire (*śivāgni*), provide a seat with the *praṇava*, and place the cooking vessel (*sthālī*) upon it. Then, [one should prepare] the flour of sacrificial rice grains (*yājñīya-dhānyataṇḍula*).

Having cast the wind and the measure that has spread out into it, one seated in the direction of Agni performs a special worship with *cālana* and so forth, offering tooth-sticks and the like, while avoiding the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as prescribed.
Having assigned the locations, then having gratified the mantras, performed the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*),
and offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), having given [the offering] to the Sun, and having sipped water, she—
having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*— gave the purifying thread (*pavitraka*) to Tārā and the others, as before.

Having entered, [one should perform] the purification (*pavitraka*) for Vāstoṣpati, Brahmā, the auspicious water-pot (*śivakumbha*), the weapon (*astra*), and the *vardhanī* vessel; then, having approached the presence of the Deity and sat upon one's own seat,
one should perform a special worship according to one's means, both for one's own form and for the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*).

Having offered the purifying thread (*pavitraka*), one should meditate upon Śiva as the essence of Time (*kālātmaka*), whose form consists of years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, moments, breaths, and so forth; who is the sole cause for the functioning of all the senses and the body;
and who is the unique witness to all deeds performed, unperformed, and abandoned.

Having taken up a purifying *pavitraka* thread, one should address the Lord (*Īśvara*), the protector of the field, the sovereign, the refuge, and the pure one, standing before the auspicious water-pot (*śivakalasa*): "Oṃ! O God, whatever has been done, left unfinished, abandoned, or maintained by you through your nature as Time (*kālātman*) within my ritual procedure—"

And it is protected by me. Let that which has been performed be auspicious and effortless; let it be honored in this inquiry by this pure Śambhu with his whole self through your will. Reciting "Oṃ pūraya 2 makha yameśvarāya svāhā," [one offers] "Oṃ hauṃ, to Śiva, the lord of the Śiva-tattva."

Salutation! Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva). Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva, the lord of the principle of the self (ātma-tattva). Having thus placed three purifiers (pavitraka) in sequence upon the top of the liṅga, one places the fourth, which consists of all principles, upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā). Oṃ.
One should offer [the oblation] with the root mantra itself, saying: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of all principles.

Then, those desiring worldly enjoyment or liberation should perform the recitation (japa) according to the sequence of the principles beginning with the Self-principle (ātmatattva). Having performed the recitation and offered praise to the altar, [one should continue] for four, three, two, or one month, or half of that, or for seven nights.

Having undertaken [the rite] for five nights, three nights, or one night, or until the conclusion of the commenced ritual, or as long as the wearing of the *pavitraka* [is prescribed], and having taken the vow regarding the reception of the Veda (*brahmagrahaṇa*)— thinking "this must be performed by me"— one should bow down, ask for forgiveness, and enter the interior of the sacrificial pavilion.
Having worshipped the guardians of the world (lokapālas) with their respective portions and having offered the purifiers (pavitrakas) to the weapons (astras),

one should approach the vicinity of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and offer four purifiers to the Blessed Lord residing in the fire according to the primary sacrifice (mūlayāga). Then, [one should worship] the fire with the [mantras of] pervasion (vyāpti).
Having restrained [the breath], one should offer oblations with the *sviṣṭakṛt* mantra. Then, having entered within and worshipped the Lord of Gods (*Deveśa*),
and having given the *pavitraka* to the Guru and to the books of the Siddhānta, one should offer the sacrificial bali to the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) and others.

"Accept, obeisance! Oṃ, accept, obeisance to Īśāna! Oṃ, accept, obeisance to Brahmā! Oṃ, accept, obeisance to Viṣṇu! Having thus cast the outer *bali* offerings in their respective directions in due order, [he offers] to the north-west with "Oṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla."

Having offered the *bali* to the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should offer the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) to fill any deficiencies in the rite, and then offer the full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). Thereafter, one should recite the *vyāhṛtis*: "Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā; Guruvaḥ svāhā;
Oṃ svaḥ svāhā; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā."

Having performed the *maṃ* and having likewise restrained the fire there, one should offer four oblations with the mantras: "Oṃ Agnaye Svāhā," "Oṃ Somāya Svāhā," "Oṃ Agnīṣomābhyām Svāhā," and "Oṃ Agnaye Sviṣṭikṛte Svāhā. Then, by means of the connection of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*), one should [unify] Śiva residing in the fire with [Śiva] situated in the mandala.

One should unite [the disciple] with Śiva. Then, having worshipped the Lord and offered the *pavitraka* (sacred thread) to the Siddhānta manuscript and the Guru, one should go outside, perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), and sequentially partake of three pure circles of cow dung, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the tooth-cleansing stick. Then, having performed the ritual rinsing, being pure—

Having spread darbha grass upon his bed, one desiring worldly enjoyment (vubhukṣu) should protect himself with three layers of sesame seeds and other substances and sleep while reciting the name of Śiva; one desiring liberation (mumukṣu) should likewise do so with sacred ash alone. Then, having risen in the morning, performed the rites of purification and bathing, and completed the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana), he should remove the remains of the previous day's offerings (nirmālya) and so forth.
Having placed the released fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka) in the mandala of the northeast corner,

having performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa), and having prepared the general offering vessel (sāmānyārghapātra), one should bathe Śiva as prescribed, perform ritual sipping of water, and perform the ritual of self-protection at the doors.
Having worshipped the door-keepers as before, one should enter through the western door,
offer a flower to Vāstoṣpati, worship the Śivakalaśa and the Vardhanī vessel,
then duly honor the guardians of the quarters (Dikpālas) together with their weapons, and worship one's own seat with the Praṇava.

Having sat down, performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the purification of the substances for the special *argha* vessel, the purification of the ritual hand, and the preparation of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and having worshipped the deity according to the daily rite (*nityavidhi*), one approaches the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), sprinkles it with water while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and [performs the rites] upon its girdles (*mekhalā*).
Having worshipped the weapons, the world-protectors, the oceans, and the seats, beginning with Brahmā as before;
having consecrated the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter as previously described; having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);

and having performed the rites such as the satiation of the mantras, one should offer the sacrificial portion (*bali*) upon the enclosing sticks and the seats, without yet performing the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*).

Having cast [the offering] from the Śiva-fire, and without performing the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*), one approaches the vicinity of Śiva; then, while the deity is indeed present, nine *liṅgas* ending with the hand are [offered] on the occasion of the occasional rite (*naimittika*). These constitute the smallest *liṅga*, measuring eight finger-breadths at its base.
By increasing [the measurement] by one unit, there are thirty-three [types]. Likewise, starting from sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), there are nine wooden lingas, ending at six cubits (*hasta*).
By increasing the smallest [measurement] by one-quarter [of its size], those too become exactly thirty-three. Alternatively, [this applies to] the fourth [type] of temple.
The length of the *liṅga* may be five or six parts; or, within the sanctum (*garbha*) of the temple, when divided into five parts, it may be three parts;
or when divided into nine parts, it may be five parts, half a part, or three intervals. This applies to the entire group of *liṅgas*, even those that are perfectly symmetrical.
Having divided half of its length into eight parts, one should worship the Linga—honored by gods and sages—with portions measuring four, five, six, three, and five [parts] respectively.
These Lingas, characterized by their width, are designated as "Anādya," "Ādya," and "Sarvasama. Thus are the Lingas defined.

These [parts] come into being. Of these, the square Brahma-section, marked by a cord at half the distance from the corner and divided into seven parts by excluding the corners—having established three parts in the middle and excluding two parts on each side—the Vaishnava section is [formed], which is octagonal. This is the station of Brahma.
Due to error or from the commencement of omitting the *aśri*, the portion for Vṛtta and Rudra [is affected].

By turning out a quarter of the width at the top of the *liṅga*, it becomes known as the *kukkuṭāṇḍa* (cock’s egg) shape. Likewise, by turning out a third part, it becomes the *ardhacandra* (half-moon).

The lotus (*puṣpa*) consists of six parts; the umbrella (*chatra*) consists of eight, being one-eighth [of the total]. When that is divided by eight, the lotus becomes fourfold by the turning of each part, known by the names Puṇḍarīka, Viśāla, Śrīvatsa, and Śatrumardana. It is drawn according to the stated measurements.
If [the line] is long, there is the destruction of wealth and a gross death; if it is very high, there is the decline of one's lineage. If it is short, there is disease.

If it is curved, there is the loss of the kingdom. If it is low, there is famine; if moderately low, there is agitation among the subjects; if it is low at the top, there is total destruction. If it is long in the portion of Rudra, there is worship.
Deficiency [is indicated by the following]. In the center, there is a long drought; below, there is the ruin of the kingdom for a long time.
[The omen] is characterized by the aforementioned marks: lines of junction, clusters of dots, pegs, stains, smoke, holes, fear, dust, the tracks of crows, and those of cats.
The base-less [pedestal] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The portion for Rudra is equal to the head [of the liṅga].

Having understood the directions, the pedestal-base, the water-channel, the entrance into the Brahma-portion, and the Brahma-stone, one should construct the raised pedestal up to the Viṣṇu-portion. Whatever merits or defects exist in the liṅga, they likewise apply to the pedestal.

Those very [rites apply here]. In that case, having performed the *hṛtya* for a *liṅga* measuring one cubit (*hasta*), and having offered the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) and performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship the maṇḍala up to the Lord (*bhagavant*) and ask for forgiveness. Then, [one should honor him] with food, clothing, and so forth.

Having worshipped the initiated [disciple], one should say: "May Sadāśiva be pleased with me. At the conclusion of the vow (*vrata*), having worshipped Śiva on the very next day, he who desires worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) should offer the vow to Śiva, saying: "O Blessed One, may this vow be effective for the attainment of my fruit. He who desires liberation (*mukti*), however, [should say] "may it be for me..."
One should announce, "May it become an obstacle to [the disciple's] karma. Then, having performed the ritual up to the libation for the mantra (*mantratarpaṇa*),
having performed the expiatory fire-oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*), having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
and having paid homage to the ashes, one should [invite] the Blessed One residing in the fire by means of the connection of the channels (*nāḍīsandhāna*).

Having conjoined [the fire] with Śiva, having extracted the mantras of the fire, having led them to the *dvādaśānta*, having established them in the heart, and having dismissed the fire, one should offer oblations to the enclosure-sticks (*paridhi*), the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*), and the two doors; then,

having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) and performed the ritual of "making all parts complete" (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one enters within and [worships] the Śiva-pitcher, the weapon-mantra, and the *vardhanī* vessel.
Having withdrawn the mantras and joined them with Śivā, he should dismiss them with the words "forgive me" while maintaining the necessary mental focus. Then,

having dismissed the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and the guardians of the gates (valāṭīs), and having taken the sacred thread (pavitraka) from the deity, he should offer that sacred thread to Caṇḍeśvara at Tricaṇḍeśvara, and present the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) and other items belonging to the sacred thread.

If, out of faith, one has performed the purification for the purpose of expiation, one should repeat the third mantra one hundred thousand times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number.
[Thus ends the ritual for the Pavitraka thread in the Siddhāntasārapaddhati composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva. || 0 ||
[Now, the procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhāvidhi):

Since the liṅga, the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and so forth serve as its substratum, their characteristics are now described. In that regard, starting from the measure of one cubit (hasta) and increasing by a quarter-cubit (pāda) up to three cubits—
There are nine liṅgas in the smallest ladle (*kaṭacchaka*);
likewise, by this same progression, up to six cubits (*hasta*) in the middle-sized ladle;
and by this same progression, from seven to nine cubits, there are also nine liṅgas in the largest ladle.
They exist. Likewise, there are others as well:
among those measuring between three and four cubits, and between six and seven cubits, there are exactly six mobile liṅgas;
thus, there are thirty-three liṅgas made of stone and made of clay. Furthermore—
The mobile liṅga made of gems or metals begins at the size of a mudga bean and extends up to nine aṅgulas;
that made of the eight metals begins at eight aṅgulas and extends up to eight aṅgulas [in width].
Having flooded the excavated pit with the water remaining in the pitcher and having bathed the spade and other implements,

one should worship them. Thereafter, having placed the full pitcher, covered with a pair of cloths, upon the lap of a Brāhmaṇa, [one should proceed] with song, instrumental music, and the like, accompanied by the Veda.
In the presence of many witnesses, he should lead [the cord] as far as the intended eastern boundary of the city.

Having stood there for a mere moment, he should cause it to revolve clockwise from the southeast (āgneya) to the northeast (īśāna). Then, on the ground of the palace, he should fix eight stakes to mark the boundary of the palace.
For the sake of determination, having placed [the markers] at the four corners and joined them with a thread, one should draw the lines with gold,
silver, pearls, parched grain, and so forth. At the center or at the cardinal points, [one should place] the syllables *vaṃ*,
*kaṃ*, *caṃ*, *taṃ*, *eṃ*, *haṃ*, *śaṃ*, and *paṃ*.

One should recognize the presence of a foreign body (*śalya*) through nine signs of inquiry: therein, if one scratches the head, there is a foreign body in the head; by that same measure, if there is no other change such as scratching elsewhere, there is a foreign body in that specific limb; and if it is of two forms, the foreign body is likewise of two forms.

Having recognized that every part of the body is subject to affliction and that the entire field [of the body] is possessed of a thorn, one should dig it up, extract the thorn, and fill it with earth— eight finger-breadths high, moistened from within,
and compacted by striking with a mallet— until it reaches the level of the third step, making it perfectly level.
Having made the ground well-constructed, very well-constructed, and smooth,

and having first established a vertical line from the southeast to the northwest due to the fear of shadows and so forth, and having laid down a horizontal line from the northeast to the southwest, one should place the joints at the intervals of six, six, and eight [units].

Having understood this, one should place Īśa in the half of the northeast corner; then, having worshipped Aparājita, Jaya, Mahendra, Ravi, Satya, and Vṛṣa at every step starting from the northeast, and having assigned Vyoman and Pāvaka to the southeast chamber,
one should worship Pūṣan, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, Yama, and Gandharva.
Having assigned Bhṛṅgin and Padika to the square in the northwestern corner, and having stationed Mṛga and Pitṛ there, [one assigns] Dvārapāla, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, Asura, Śoṣa,
and the others to the square in the northwestern corner, and Roga and Tāpa.

The temple (prāsāda) is four cubits in width; or else, it is three, four, five, or six times the measurement of the liṅga in width. The Bhūmija [temple] is three times the height of the temple, or one and a half times twice [the height].

The *nāgara* style has a double *śikhara* (spire) and a *valabhī* (pavilion roof). For temples made of iron or wood, starting from the smallest *liṅga* and measuring four cubits (*hasta*) and so forth, the temple (*prāsāda*) should be constructed with a width ranging up to thirty cubits. For those made of jewels, it should be according to the specific requirements of the material itself.
Now, one desiring to build a palace should first acquire a site that has been thoroughly examined.

In this regard, ground that is sweet in taste, possesses the smell of clarified butter (*ājya*), and is fragrant belongs to a Brāhmaṇa; that which is red, possesses the smell of blood, and is bitter belongs to a Kṣatriya; that which is yellow, possesses the smell of grain, and is pungent belongs to a Vaiśya; and that which is black, possesses the smell of meat, and is acrid belongs to a Śūdra.

Having gone today to a Śūdra’s [well], O Bhīṣma, it is said that water is considered impure due to its connection with lamps, fuel, and so forth; it should be examined. In this regard, a pit one cubit deep is dug, and if it is filled again with the earth excavated from it, that is mediocre. Where the excavated earth remains [exceeding the hole], that is excellent.
A pit that is not filled with earth is the lowest; one that is filled with water up to the depth of a hundred paces, until it is seen completely full,
is superior.

The middle [wick] is deficient by one finger-breadth; it is called "near" when it is deficient by many finger-breadths. Having placed raw [butter] upon the top of a jar or a full vessel, and having lit four wicks—white, red, yellow, and [black]—in the four directions, [one performs the rite] beginning with Tatpuruṣa.

If one should see [the fire] burning until the end of the oil, having been consecrated with mantras, then one should know that the ground for all castes is auspicious. As long as the earth remains unextinguished, it is considered auspicious;
thus, having examined the ground and determined it to be auspicious, one should construct upon it the pavilion together with the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as prescribed.

Having caused [the image] to be made, and having performed the ritual beginning with the worship of the gatekeepers and ending with the satiation by mantras, one should offer a thousand oblations with the *ātma-ghorāstra* mantra. Then, one should place five jars upon seven kinds of grain, filled with meritorious water (*puṇyodaka*) and containing excellent medicinal herbs and gems.

Having worshipped the interior of the temple— a womb adorned with mangoes, *aśvattha* trees, and so forth, its face beautified by sprouts, *bījapūra* fruits, and the like, covered with a pair of white cloths, with a white sacrificial ladle (*śruk*) and thread around its neck, and presided over by the Blessed One with his own person— [one should perform the rite] at the moment of the auspicious conjunction (*lagnakāla*).
Having poured water from a pitcher into the central spot,
[he should do so] in the east, west, south, north, and the northeast as well. Then, having dug in the central spot,
he should take earth from there and cast it toward the southwest direction.

Having caused a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) to be constructed in front of the temple, increasing in size from twelve cubits down to two cubits in successive stages, and having established there a bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*) or a consecration pavilion (*adhivāsanamaṇḍapa*) to its east, north, or northeast, the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall sit therein.

Having offered ornaments and other gifts to those possessing physical forms, one should take the vessel containing the *arghya* water and place five, six, or seven cubit-long arches (*toraṇa*) upon the smaller liṅgas; for the others, they should increase by eight or four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). These should be produced from the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, or *plakṣa* trees.
Starting from the east, having installed the arches known as Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, and Ardha—

which are purified by the Astra-mantra and enveloped in armor— using the Praṇava, and having worshipped them with their own heart-mantras and names, one should [install] Nandi and Mahākāla on the two branches of that [eastern arch], and Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka [on the others].

Having worshipped Vṛṣaskati and the goddess Caṇḍī by their respective names, one should [place] upon banners of red, black, dark-blue cloud-color, and yellow lotus-color the emblems known as the trident, thunderbolt, spear, staff, sword, noose, banner, and mace, for Īśvara and Indra.
Having worshipped the weapons of the world-protectors: the Brahmā-weapon, the lotus, in the northeast;
the Viṣṇu-weapon, the discus, in the southwest, on a blue-flowered [lotus] (atasīpuṣpavarṇa); and in the center, upon a white seat or a banner, either the Pāśupata weapon or the Aghora weapon.
And having entered without [specific] cause, he then sits upon the altar facing the east.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), completed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and prepared the vessel of honor (*arghapātra*),
he places the *ārā* on his head and takes a hand for the rite consisting of thirty-two *darbha* blades.
Having prepared a sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) consecrated with mantras fashioned by a merchant,
and having established it within the five compartments consisting of the *maṇḍala*, one should place a vessel filled with milk in the eastern *śivatattva* compartment,
curd in the southern *sadāśivatattva* compartment, and ghee in the [southeastern] *vidyātattva* compartment.
One should place ghee in the form of fire in the eastern compartment, nectar-like cow dung in the western compartment representing the principle of Time (kāla-tattva),

and gems and so forth along with cow urine in the northern compartment representing the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva), consecrating them respectively with the limbs of the mantra and the root mantra.

Having properly prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scattered them, one should consecrate them with mantras. Then, facing the northeast within the pavilion located in the southwest, one should perform the rites of inspection,
sprinkling, pouring water, digging, scattering, leveling, and moistening the ground.

Having purified [the site] with rites ending in sweeping, smearing, and the consecration as a vajra, accompanied by their respective mantras, and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should visualize [the ground] as consisting of blazing weapons,
perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), and assign the positions starting from the chief Nāga, Bhalvāṭha, Loma, Giri, and ending with Āditya.
One should worship the goddess situated in the half of the northeast corner. In the center is Brahmā; in his other directions [are as follows]:
Āpa and Āpavatsa in the east; Marīci on six squares in the southeast;
Savitṛ and Sāvitrī in the south; Vivasvat in the southwest; Indra and Indrajaya in the west.
Having worshipped Mitra in the northwest, Rudra and Rudradāsa in the north,

and [the deities] beginning with Āpa and Vatsa in sequence starting from the northeast (Īśāna) with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, curd, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth, one should worship Carakī, Skanda, Vidārī, Anyā, Pūtanā, and Jambhā in the directions beginning with Īśāna.
One should worship the eight deities within and outside the *pilipiccha* [circular diagram] facing away from oneself. || 0 ||
In the center of the eighty-one squares of the *vāstu* diagram, Brahmā occupies nine squares; Marīci and the others occupy six squares each;
Āpavatsa and the others occupy two squares each; and the external deities are as before, including Vatsara, Aṅka, and the rest.
Having worshipped the *vāstu* and avoided the vital points (*marmans*) and so forth, one should lay the foundation stone for the house.
Now, the characteristic of *pratiṣṭhā*: therein, in the middle of the cavity of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*),
which has the characteristic of being raised in the form of a vulva (*bhaga*) and is the nature of the power of self-concealment (*svaguptakriyāśakti*),
one performs the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) by joining [the deity] in the position below the characteristic of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
The ritual application of the two liṅgas and the pedestal is established according to the prescribed rule.
And that method is fivefold therein: *pratiṣṭhā*, *sthāpana*, *utthāpana*, *āsthāpana*, and [the others].

Among these, *pratiṣṭhā* is that wherein, having clearly placed the *liṅga* upon the *brahmaśilā* and having performed the binding of the pedestal (*pīṭhabandha*), the union is effected with the *piṇḍikā*.
Where a stone, metal, or wooden linga is divided into five parts or three parts, and two or even one part is placed upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā), that is *sthāpana*;
whereas when it is not divided from the pedestal and is consecrated as an undivided whole, that is *sthitasthāpana*.

The restoration of what is decayed is the re-establishment (*utthāpana*). Having placed the manifest form of Rudra upon the water-pedestal (*jalapīṭha*), it is consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ*-mantras; that is taken away, and then the installation (*sthāpana*) occurs.
Thus, there are five forms of installation for Maheśvara, due to his being both manifest and unmanifest.
Because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are manifest, [their installation] consists of two types: *āsthāpana* (establishment) and *utthāpana* (raising).
Among those, for liṅgas measuring from eight to nine cubits, [the measurement] is three cubits in the middle; for other liṅgas measuring four cubits and so forth, it is two cubits.
In accordance with the increase [of the ritual stages]:
clarified butter in the south, cow-dung in the west, cow-urine in the north,
water, golden ornaments, various kinds of jewelry, incense, honey, and garments.

Having arranged the collection of causal substances in the compartments— namely, *nairāñjana* in the southeast (*āgneya*), *nairitya* (? in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), *saṃgraha* in the northwest (*vāyavya*), and *kuṅkuma* in the northeast (*īśāna*)— one should place milk, *āmala*, fragrance, gem, fruit, flower, grain, and medicinal water [in the remaining compartments].

Having placed the jars marked with their respective signs, sprinkled them with the *astra* mantra, and veiled them with the *kavaca* mantra; having worshipped them with their own names and conceptualized them as the oceans such as the salt ocean (*kṣāra-samudra*), one should also arrange other jars on the outside and likewise the eight stones marked with the [eight] world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Having worshipped and satisfied [the deities] with oblations of sesame and ghee, and having approached the stone with the essence [of the mantra],

one should perform recitation according to the number of oblations. Then, touching the base of the stone while joined with the *śamalena* [mantra], one should sprinkle it again with the water from the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*).

Having approached the vicinity of the *kuṇḍa* and sat down, one should perform the union of the two principles (*tattvas*) by saying "Salutation to the Self-principle (*ātmatattva*) and the Knowledge-principle (*vidyātattva*"). Then, having established and worshipped Viṣṇu— the presiding deity of the Knowledge-principle— along with his forms (*mūrti*) and the guardians of those forms (*mūrtipās*), [one should offer oblations] with sesame seeds, ghee, and the essence [of the materials].
Having satisfied the knowers [of the mantras] according to the number of oblations, one should go near the stone and perform recitation (*japa*). Then,

touching the middle part of the stone with the middle part of the *kuśa* grass and sprinkling it with water from the *śānti*-pot, one should return to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and sit down.

Having recited "Obeisance to Vidyātattva and Śivatattva," and having established the presiding deities of the Śiva-tattva along with Rudra as the embodied form and the guardians of that form, and having gratified them with oblations, one should perform the recitation (japa) near the stone according to the number of fire-offerings (homa), and touch the top of the stone with the tip of the hook (aṅkuśa).

He should cause the command of Śiva to be heard: "O Lords of the Tattvas, together with the Tattva-mūrtis and their presiding deities, you must remain present at the command of Śiva. Having arrived and offered a hundred, a thousand, or half [of the offerings], and having completed the ritual actions, the Ācārya, with the root mantra, [should perform] the *pūrṇāhuti*.
The personified deities (mūrtidharas) should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with their respective mantras according to their directions and offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Then, having performed the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa), they should take the stone and the pitchers, go to the pit (dromāda), and having offered a hundred oblations for the support of the foundation (svādhāra-śanti), [they should recite] "Oṃ."

Having placed the *kumbha* with the mantra "anantāyaṃ ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha ccha na," one should contemplate the pervasion of the *adhvapada* (the stages of the path) at the time of the *lagna*.

Having scattered the *vikira* offerings and then gathered them back with a bunch of darbha grass, having placed them in the northeast corner of the altar, and having brought one vessel made of gold or another metal and filled it with filtered water,
having offered a seat upon the collected *vikiras*, he should place the vessel containing the manifested form there.

Having fully worshipped the Blessed One together with his retinue, one should adorn both the Vardhanī vessel to His right and the Astra-mantra with a pair of white garments and other offerings; then, at the eastern gate, one should place Praśānta and Śiśira,
at the southern [gate] Parjanya and Āśoka, and at the western [gate] Bhūta, Sañjīva, and Amṛta.
Then, having placed ten jars presided over by the world-protectors ending with Viṣṇu,
and having rotated the jar together with the *piṇḍikā* and the *vardhanī* through the gateway, [he says]:
"O Śakra, you must remain vigilant until the end of the sacrifice in order to pacify obstacles in this direction."
Having given the command to the world-protectors (lokapālas) in this sequence— "It must be done by the command of Śiva"—

and having worshipped the [central] seat, the *vardhanī* vessel, and the *kumbha*, and having placed the Lord's sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) upon the *kumbha*, he should establish the supportless vessel (*nirādhāra*).

Having driven away all remaining obstacles from every direction with weapons arisen from the *vardhanī*, the seat, and the *vikīra* [mantras], and having approached the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he performs the rites beginning with the inspection and ending with the generation of the fire;
then, having divided the fire into nine or five parts, he pacifies those situated in the directions.

Having cast the middle [portion] into the pits, having kindled the fire in one's own pit, having worshipped the Blessed One, and having gratified him with the eleven-fold mantra-rite, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* offering; then, for each pit, one should consecrate the peace-vases (*śāntikumbha*) at the tip of the weapon-mantra or with the root-mantra.

One should not perform [the rite] with the *saṃpāta* oblations. Having gone [to the site], one should sprinkle the *liṅga* and other objects with that water, part by part, for the purpose of bringing the mantra into proximity. Then, in the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*), one should arrange a nine-celled grid; in the center is the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), in the east the principle of Sadāśiva, and in the southeast...

Having placed the principle of Īśvara in the south, the principle of Vidyā in the southwest, the principle of Māyā in the west, the principle of Kāla in the northwest, the principle of Niyati in the north, the principle of Puruṣa in the northeast,
and the principle of Prakṛti in the northeast, one should also fill the center with milk.

Having joined [the breaths] and placed them in the sky, O Lord of the fifteen worlds, and having performed the expiatory *homa* which removes the defects of speech, mind, and body, and having offered the *bali* to the world-protectors, one should dismiss the sacrifice with the words "May you forgive me."
[Thus ends the ritual for the installation of the pedestal in the *Siddhāntasārapaddhati* composed by the great king of kings, the illustrious Bhojadeva. || 0 ||

Now follows the ritual procedure for the installation of a *liṅga*. Therein, having prepared two pavilions as before, and having constructed nine, five, or one sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should assemble the group of officiants. According to the number of pits, one should procure the large and small ladles (*śruk-śruva*), vessels for sesame seeds, vessels for the *arghya* offering, vessels for clarified butter (*ājya*), a bell, incense, and fire-kindling materials.

The vessel for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the pot for the sacrificial porridge (caru), the Śiva-pitcher, the pitcher for the weapon (astra), the vardhanikā, the Nidrā-pitcher, the vessel for the minor limbs (vyaṅga), the peace-pitcher (śānti-kumbha)— all these up to the end [of the sequence]— as well as the pitchers for the door-keepers, the world-protectors (lokapāla), and the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara), should be made of copper; those made of clay may also be used.

For the purpose of bathing, one should take eight types of earth from a mountain peak, a riverbank, the middle of a sacred field, the tusk of an elephant, the horn of a bull, the root of a *śara* grass, an anthill, and a holy ford (*tīrtha*), as well as water from those same holy fords. One should also take the barks of the *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *jantu*, and *āmra* trees, along with cow’s urine.
Cow dung, milk, clarified butter, all medicinal herbs, auspicious seats, two silver vessels, two golden probes,
all seeds beginning with the letter *vī*, two types of *bhūtikā* incense, a sword, a razor, and household utensils.

Having brought in abundance sandals, a canopy, houses with multi-colored banners, *tejocandrovaka*, sesame oil, ghee, sugar-candy, *guggulu* resin, *viśvapatra*, sandalwood, saffron, fine cloth, betel leaves, and so forth, [he should proceed] to the north.
Having placed the eight [vessels] on the altar in their proper order according to the ritual manual,
having performed the entry into the pavilion as before, and having sat down upon the altar and purified the body, one should place a white turban, consecrated with the root mantra, upon the head.
Having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), beginning from the placement of the sustaining power (dhāra-śakti) up to the final transformation into the Supreme (parasīkaraṇa),
one should draw forth the supreme light from the space of the heart, place it in one's own eyes,
and having gazed upon the collection of substances, [purify] the argha vessel by means of burning, leaping upward, and so forth.

Having consecrated [the vessel] and filled it with water in the form of nectar (*amṛta*), having worshipped the Blessed One together with his limbs, and having performed the ritual actions from the *karmahasta* onwards up to the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with mantras,
one should bring [the deity] to the northern altar (*uttaravedikā*), perform purification, and [anoint him] with the *ācārya*-mudrās.
Having performed the ritual bath with a group reciting the *kathā*, using cow’s urine mixed with water, cow dung mixed with water,
and blood, and having reflected upon the nine or five [mantras], one should bring a copper vessel and fill it.
One should commence the ritual bathing with earth, with a group of medicinal herbs, with cow’s urine, and then with water;

having bathed [the deity] with cow dung, then with the eight [substances], and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, one should clothe [the deity] in red garments and circumambulate the pavilion.

Having caused [the disciple] to enter through the western door and having placed him upon the bed on the altar, one should place a sleep-pitcher near his head; then, having covered him with a cloth consecrated with the *varma* mantra, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), [one should contemplate] the path beginning with earth and ending with *buddhi*.
Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the thread-sections (*tantrikhaṇḍa*), one should meditate upon them: therein, the *ātmatattva* ending with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*);

the *vidyātattva* ending with *sanman*; the *śivatattva* ending with the *ahaṅkāra* and *buddhi*; and the lords of these three principles—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara—as well as Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, Sun, Water, and Wind.
Having installed the eight forms known as Candra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra,
Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and the one named Bhīma— the eight lords of the forms (mūrtīśvarāṣṭaka)—
and having restrained [the breath] with a spittle-spray, one should worship them upon the stone slab.

All the [deities] beginning with the Directions (Digvādi) and the [deities of the] stones (Śilāsuta) should be installed individually in their respective directions; having installed and restrained the two forms of one's own direction, one should worship them. Then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and sat down, one should [offer] in the middle of the pit: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti)."

Having worshipped [the deity] and offered three oblations to Śakti, one should offer with this: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the self (ātmatattva); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self; Oṃ dāṃ, obeisance to the form Kṣmā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the lord of the form Kṣā. Thus.

The lords of the forms [are installed] by way of the path. Having uttered the mantra "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva," one should install the stone with a prostration. Then, in the pits of the eastern and other directions: "Oṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Indra"; "Oṃ ruṃ, obeisance to Agni"; "Oṃ druṃ, obeisance to Yama"; "Oṃ ṣūṃ..."
Homage to Nairṛti! Oṃ vūṃ, homage to Varuṇa! Oṃ yūṃ, homage to Vāyu!
Oṃ sūṃ, homage to Soma! Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Īśāna! With these mantras of the World-Protectors (lokeśa), one should prepare copper jars filled with ghee and honey, well-secured with fine thread.

Having placed their necks [into the holes] and fixed stone slabs over them, one should install the fourfold [deities] beginning with Dharma as the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of the stone slabs; then, having performed the *argha* offering for the upper path (*ūrdhvādhvan*) consisting of milk, sesame, white mustard, barley, and rice, one should perform the *ācamana*.
Having given [the offerings] and worshipped with the root mantra, one should raise [the deity] with the heart-mantra, place him upon the chariot,
circumambulate the city, the town, the temple,
or the pavilion, and cast gold, garments, jewels, and *karavaka* fruits before the pavilion.
Having removed [the deity] from the chariot with the *hṛdaya* mantra, having caused him to enter the pavilion through the western door,

and having brought him to the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*), one should provide a seat upon the couch using either the general mantra or the *śiras* mantra; then, having placed a pillow with the *śikhā* mantra, one should cover it with a cloth over which the *varma* mantra has been recited.
Having covered [the deity] and offered the food offering (naivedya), one should give a vessel-cover; then, having given a pestle, a mortar, a stone, a broom, a water-wheel (yantrikā), a bowl,
and other household utensils, one should place a vessel of honey and clarified butter at the feet while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).

Having established the residence with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra near the head, one should worship the sleep-pitcher (nidrākumbha) with a sword [as its insignia], like the Śiva-pitcher; then, having offered flowers and protective threads (*pratisara*) to the eight pitchers of the Vidyeśvaras in the directions and to those who indicate the divisions, one should construct a rampart with *abhūti*, darbha grass, and sesame seeds.
Having fully worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), one should install the principles (*tatva*) and their presiding deities (*mūrti-mūrtipā*).
Therein, having meditated upon the entire collection of the *ātmatattva* ending with *māyā*, [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ*. [And so on] up to Sadāśiva.

Following the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva): Oṃ Hīṃ, salutation to the principle of knowledge. Oṃ Hīṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the principle of knowledge. Pervading up to the end of the principle of Śiva: Oṃ Hūṃ, salutation to the principle of the universe (viśva-tattva). Oṃ Hūṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the principle of Śiva. Thus.

Having placed the *ātmatattva* in the portion of Brahmā, the *vidyātattva* in the portion of Viṣṇu, and the *śivatattva* in the portion of Rudra, one should assign the forms (*mūrti*) and the formless (*amūrti*) as pervading each respective principle (*tattva*) across these three principles. *Oṃ hāṃ kṣmā mūrtaye namaḥ.* *Oṃ hāṃ...*
Salutation to Śarva, the Lord of the Earth-form; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Fire-form;
Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Paśupati, the Lord of the Fire-form; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Sacrificer-form; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Ugra, the Lord of the Sacrificer-form.
Homage!
On the second altar, the Guru should draw the marks with a golden stylus;
there, having divided the portion for worship into three parts, he should set aside one part at the top.

One should introduce the characteristic mark in the form of a *liṅga* using two parts; the circle is formed by a line extending beyond half [the diameter]. For the goddess of the *liṅga*, having divided [the height] into sixteen parts and set aside one part, the width between the two lines is to be measured with two parts; and the excavation of the line is likewise [to be measured].

The measurement for the width is as follows: for a nine-cubit *liṅga*, it is by means of eight [parts]. For *liṅgas* of eight cubits and so forth, it is determined by the rule of three (*trairāśika*). Alternatively, a ninth part of a barleycorn (*yava*) is a "barley-part" (*yavāṃśa*);
as many barley-parts as there are finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in the portion for worship, so many [finger-breadths] are there.
The measurement of the characteristic line (*lakṣaṇarekhā*) is as follows: the wing-field (*pakṣakṣetra*) is divided into three parts;

from the wing-line thread, having set aside one and a half parts below, for one desiring the continuity of the kingdom, the descent of the wing-line should be performed by means of a circle (*bhrama*).
On the back of the two lines, whether their sum or their difference is divided ninefold,
one should discard two parts below and perform a circular rotation (*bhrama*) at the point where the side-lines descend;
or [the circle] may be divided sixteenfold.

Having abandoned two parts, the artisan should, by means of nine, twelve, or fourteen rotations, bring forth the line of the wings; or, in the case of images, he should perform the opening of the eyes according to the sequence of the corners and edges. Having carved it with that tool, [he should anoint it] with ghee and honey.

Having filled the vessel, the probe, and other implements with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra and given them to the artisan, one should again seat [the image] upon its throne. Then, eight or four women whose husbands are living should touch it with a red thread, or with *dāruharidrā*, oil, and turmeric; and the *nīrājana* ceremony and other rites should be performed.
They should perform the ritual actions. Immediately thereafter, having struck [the image] with the Astra-mantra, protected it with the Varma-mantra, and veiled it,
one should worship it with either the common mantra or its own specific mantra, and then commence the ritual bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)—
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey— along with water containing the four [other] cow-products.

Having bathed [the deity] with jars of milk, water, and so forth, fashioned as the ocean and consecrated by the respective mantras of their own forms, one should smear [the deity] with sandalwood paste and other unguents,
clothe [him] in two red garments, perform the lustration (*nīrājana*), and [offer] *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water.

Then, having touched the root of the *kuśa* grass at the base of the *liṅga* with the root mantra, one should sprinkle it with water from the peaceful *kumbha*. Again, having gone near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the *ātmatattva* and the *vidyātattva*. Thus, by way of both pure and impure forms.
Having made the *tattva* of ignorance blind, one should awaken the *tattva* of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*).

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *tattva* of knowledge" and "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the *tattva* of knowledge," one should perform the offering of oblations (*āhuti*) ending with *svāhā*. Then, [one should worship] the eight forms (*mūrti-aṣṭaka*) individually.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), worshipped with offerings, and gratified with oblations (āhuti) at the liṅga:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sun-form (arka-mūrti). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the presiding lord of the Sun-form.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Water-form (jala-mūrti). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhava, the presiding lord of the Water-form."

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna, the lord of the form of Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Indu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahādeva, the lord of the form of Indu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Kha.
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīma, the lord of the [Viṣṇu] form.

Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of the forms and the guardians of the forms, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) upon the pedestal to the north of the liṅga by this path, while Viṣṇu restrains [the breath].

And [one should place it] upon the Brahma-stone situated at the base of the *liṅga*. However, within that [stone], one should install the three powers known as Action (*kriyā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), and Will (*icchā*) by presiding over them through their respective principles (*tatva*). [Recite: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Principle of the Self (Ātmatattva)*; *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sovereign of the Principle of the Self (Ātmatattvādhipā)*.

Salutation to her. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sovereign lady of the principle of knowledge, the power of gnosis (*jñānaśakti*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sovereign lady of the principle of Śiva, the will (*icchā*).

Salutation!
